items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Canada hasn’t yet closed door on U.S. trade deal ahead of midterms
items.description: Canadian officials haven’t ruled out the possibility of a snap trade deal with the United States ahead of next month’s midterm elections, according to sources with direct knowledge of the talks.
items._ogDesc: Canadian officials haven’t ruled out the possibility of a snap trade deal with the United States ahead of next month’s midterm elections, according to sources with direct knowledge of the talks.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Canadian officials haven’t ruled out the possibility of a snap trade deal with the United States ahead of next month’s midterm elections, according to sources with direct knowledge of the talks. Though they cautioned that the hope remains faint.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and Canadian Ambassador to the U.S. Mark Wiseman briefed Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations on the state of play in a Thursday morning meeting, according to four sources with knowledge of the call.

It marked the group’s first meeting since Sept. 4.

The briefing comes a day after Carney said he spoke with U.S. President Donald Trump “for quite some time” on Wednesday morning. Carney said the two leaders discussed trade, the Iran war and the Middle East, though his office issued no formal readout of the call.

One source with direct knowledge of the Thursday advisory committee call and a separate one involving U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick told CTV News the trade discussions were “moving,” though cautioned nothing may come of that.

At Thursday’s meeting with the advisory committee, the four sources said Wiseman told the 24-member group that the public opinion tide in the U.S. was finally turning in Canada’s favour and that the federal government is seeing support grow across the U.S.

That message was echoed separately by an industry source who told CTV News that the tariff dispute with Canada is resonating with voters in the U.S. midterms and the issue is coming up in races even outside of border states.

Separately, LeBlanc’s message to the advisory committee was that anything could happen before the midterms, the sources said. They added that the minister referenced the pressure that the White House is under as successive polls show an increasingly hostile electorate and eroding prospects for the governing Republicans.

Two of the sources said LeBlanc told the advisory committee, “anything is possible.” That sentiment was echoed by a Canadian official who spoke with CTV News this week.

CTV News is not identifying the sources or official because they were not authorized to disclose details of confidential discussions.

The sources were careful not to overstate the message from the federal officials, adding that their general takeaway was that a deal is in no way guaranteed or even expected, but is not entirely impossible.

LeBlanc’s office declined to makes comments to CTV News on Thursday.

Canada’s Chief Trade Negotiator Janice Charette was also at the advisory committee meeting, according to a readout sent by the government Thursday. However, the statement makes no mention of the potential opening for a deal with the White House.

“Committee members discussed the ongoing impact of U.S. tariffs on their regions, businesses or sectors and shared their insights,” the readout said.

Charette later spoke at a Thursday afternoon panel at the Toronto Global Forum. She was careful in her characterization of the current state of talks, saying “pens are down and the doors are open,” while adding that she and LeBlanc have “regular and frequent conversations” with their respective counterparts.

“We’re trying to stabilize the relationship because we are not in a position where it is stable right now,” she said.

Charette cautioned the Toronto business crowd that Canada does not expect to go back to tariff-free trade with the U.S.

“We had tariff-free trade; that was the best. I don’t think we’re going back,” she said.

Talks between the two countries abruptly ended in August when Carney called Canadian negotiators back, which resulted in the White House imposing a fresh round of tariffs.

At the time, the prime minister said the Trump administration had asked for too much and offered too little in its negotiations to avert the August tariffs from the White House.

“You’re at war when you get attacked,” Carney said on Aug. 22. “We got attacked.”

Since then, the Americans have been trying to shift the blame for the trade dispute between the two countries. On Tuesday U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra told an industry event in Ottawa that from his perspective “we’re not in a trade war.”

“We don’t view the relationship as ruptured, and I know that the Canadians look at it differently,” he added.

With files from CTV News’ Stephanie Ha and Mike Le Couteur

items._ogDesc: Lululemon Athletica Inc. is appointing a former member of its executive team to its board to appease the retailer’s founder.
items.body:
VANCOUVER — Lululemon Athletica Inc. is appointing a former member of its executive team to its board to appease the retailer’s founder.

The Vancouver-based apparel company says Tara Poseley, who served as the company’s chief product officer from 2013 to 2015, joined its board effective Monday.

Poseley has more than 30 years of experience across specialty retail, apparel and beauty, the company said, having most recently served as chief executive of Paula’s Choice Skincare from 2016 to 2023.

Before her first stint with Lululemon, she was senior vice-president and president of Kmart Apparel from 2010 to 2013. She also spent nearly 15 years at Gap Inc. where she held senior roles across product and marketing.

  • Latest updates on company news here

“I am honoured to join Lululemon’s board at this pivotal time for the company,” said Poseley in a news release.

“I have a deep appreciation for Lululemon’s culture of innovation and commitment to creating exceptional products and guest experiences. I look forward to working with my fellow directors to support the Lululemon leadership team as it builds on the company’s strong foundation and advances its strategic priorities.”

Lululemon promised in May to appoint a director with product and brand expertise in apparel by Oct. 1 as part of a deal to end a public spat with founder Chip Wilson.

To get Wilson to stop publicly disparaging the company for about 18 months, Lululemon also agreed to add former ESPN chief marketing officer Laura Gentile and ex-On chief executive Marc Maurer to its board.

Wilson spent the end of last year and the beginning of this year at odds with Lululemon, which he accused of failing to keep up with trendy competitors.

Since the company and Wilson reached an agreement, former Nike executive Heidi O’Neill has taken Lululemon’s helm in September and shook up its leadership ranks in October. Poseley’s appointment brings the Lululemon board to 13 directors, 12 of whom are independent, the company said.

“Tara is a proven leader whose experience will further strengthen the board’s expertise across product innovation, brand strategy, operational excellence, and consumer-focused growth,” said O’Neill in a news release.

“Her insights and guidance will be invaluable as we put product, design, and innovation at the centre of how we operate to deliver on the company’s next chapter of success.”

Wilson said in a statement that Poseley “brings deep product expertise and understands what makes Lululemon special.”

“Her appointment is another positive step toward strengthening the company’s product-first vision and creating long-term value for shareholders,” he said.

items.title: Sharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jump
items.description: The latest shudder for stocks in the artificial intelligence industry pulled markets lower worldwide, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May.

items._ogDesc: The latest shudder for stocks in the artificial intelligence industry pulled markets lower worldwide, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May.
items.body:
NEW YORK — The latest shudder for stocks in the artificial intelligence industry pulled markets lower worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran.

The S&P 500 fell 1.2 per cent for its worst day since July, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.6 per cent. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the U.S. market, where the majority of stocks actually rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11 points, or less than 0.1 per cent.

AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build data centers and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that their prices shot too high following a yearslong frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8 per cent.

It gave a range for its forecast for profit this quarter whose midpoint was slightly below analysts’ expectations. Its stock also came into the day with a 52.4 per cent surge for the year so far, nearly quadruple the gain for the overall S&P 500, leaving plenty of room for potential disappointment.

Other big tech stocks likewise fell following quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.

Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7 per cent after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it’s creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.

Tesla fell 3.1 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.

The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4 per cent. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower.

CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1 per cent.

The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where indexes are full of players in the industry. South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5 per cent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3 per cent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7 per cent.

Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped 4 per cent to US$113.17 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s shot up from less than US$97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.

  • Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4 per cent. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or U.S. indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.

Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.

Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong U.S. economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the U.S. bond market recently to their highest levels in decades.

But U.S. yields nevertheless fell sharply Thursday in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury tumbled to 4.97 per cent from 5.13 per cent late Wednesday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market.

Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the U.S. economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country.

  • Latest updates on investing here

That solid economy has helped U.S. companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the U.S. stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. Two out of every three stocks within the S&P 500 rose Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks.

Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses Thursday.

CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expects “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.6 per cent.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 93.74 points to 7,663.43. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11.89 to 52,867.98, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 694.00 to 26,008.86.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Business Writer Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report.

items.title: ‘Potentially irreversible harm’: Scientists sound alarm on PM Carney’s Bill C-39
items.description: More than 50 of Canada’s top scientists and scholars warn that Bill C-39 must be amended, or the federal government is risking ‘potentially irreversible harm’ to the environment.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney delivers opening remarks ahead of the Metis Major Projects Summit at the Royal Canadian Geographical Society in Ottawa, on Thursday, Aug. 7, 2025. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Spencer Colby]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Spencer Colby</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: More than 50 of Canada’s top scientists and scholars warn that Bill C-39 must be amended, or the federal government is risking ‘potentially irreversible harm’ to the environment.
items.body:
OTTAWA - More than 50 of Canada’s top scientists and scholars are warning that Prime Minister Mark Carney’s marquee legislation aimed at fast-tracking major projects needs to be amended, or the federal government is risking “costly and potentially irreversible harm,” to the environment.

In an open letter published Thursday, 56 fellows from the Royal Society of Canada outline six specific amendments they say need to be made to Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act.

The scientific experts write that while they support the bill’s central aim of streamlining project assessments, there are several clauses within the legislation that need to be altered or scrapped entirely.

They say the changes are needed for the government to keep its promise to protect species at risk, delicate ecosystems, natural resources and human well-being.

“Bill C-39, as drafted, really puts aside a lot of the environmental regulations and laws that we have in place in Canada to protect nature and protect our waters, protect our air,” said Dr. Sarah Otto in an interview with CTV News.

Otto, one of the signatories and a zoology professor at the University of British Columbia, said the speed at which the bill is moving was a key motivator for the coalition to come together over the past week and produce the letter. It has since been submitted as a brief to key parliamentarians.

“These harms, oftentimes can’t be fixed, and so we’re really borrowing from the natural resources of future generations to pay for our economic growth right now,” she said.

While the open letter was signed by Royal Society fellows, the organization was not involved in organizing or mobilizing it, a spokesperson told CTV News.

“We are proud to be an organization that brings together many of Canada’s leading scholars, and we support our members in drawing on their expertise to contribute to important public discussions and work toward better outcomes for Canada,” said Royal Society of Canada President Françoise Baylis in an emailed statement.

Alarms sounded, but bill speeding ahead

The omnibus legislation proposing to accelerate the regulatory approval process for nation-building energy and infrastructure projects while addressing labour uncertainty, was tabled on the first day of the fall sitting. Three weeks later it cleared its first parliamentary hurdle.

When it was presented, in a press release, the government touted the bill as “the most comprehensive and ambitious reform to Canada’s ability to get big things built in a generation.”

Despite assertions from senior government officials and federal ministers that the bill upholds environmental standards and Indigenous rights, there’s been considerable pushback.

“That’s not what this bill does,” Otto said. “It does not maintain our environmental standards. It lowers them, sidesteps them, or allows ministers to dismiss the conditions that are imposed on projects to make sure that they don’t damage and harm our environment.”

In the days following Bill C-39 being introduced, climate activists brought their discontent right to Parliament Hill, resulting in several people including seniors being arrested for trespassing.

“The prime minister is rightly considering how do we balance our books, how do we make sure people are employed and that is really important across this country. But there’s also environmental books, our natural heritage, what sustains us and the species that we share this country with,” said Otto.

“Those are the environmental books, and I don’t think those are being balanced.”

Labour groups have sounded alarms over changes to the Canada Labour Code rules around collective bargaining included in the bill, which they say will have adverse consequences for workers and strip them of their right to strike.

However, business and industry stakeholders have welcomed the legislative package, which also proposes to create zones of “national interest,” and ensure federal assessments of new projects take no longer than one year and are co-ordinated under a new streamlined process.

So far, it’s largely been these pro-commerce and manufacturing voices that have been given a platform to speak to the bill, in front of the special committee struck to study it on an accelerated timeline. Otto said the experts behind the letter have requested to appear as witnesses, but they haven’t been invited, yet.

MP panel studying C-39 lacks opposition

The bill has been sent to a specially-constructed House Committee, where MPs will focus exclusively on the legislation and no other issue, unlike standing committees, which must juggle multiple bills and studies at the same time.

Given the legislation’s split focus, creating a dedicated committee rather than sending it to the labour, environment, finance or energy-focused committees appears to be an effort by the government to take the path of least resistance.

Of the 12 members tasked with studying the legislation, 11 of them have already voted in favour of it. The sole member of Parliament that voted against the legislation at second reading is Bloc Quebecois MP Gabriel Ste-Marie. Both the Liberals and Conservatives are fully backing it.

Neither Green Party MP Elizabeth May nor any NDP MPs were invited to join the committee, despite seeking an exception that would allow them to participate without official party status.

“The only vehicle open to us as parliamentarians is to amend the bill, but that process is severely limited,” said NDP Parliamentary Leader Don Davies in an interview with CTV News.

“The committee stage is the only stage of the process where Canadians get to weigh in… and it’s a very vital part because very often, through listening to Canadians, you understand the flaws of the bill, and that can often form the basis for amending it to improving it.”

However, in this case the Liberals have limited the amount of time to hear from witnesses they haven’t hand-selected, to eight hours. Davies said the “inescapable” conclusion from the decision is that Carney isn’t interested in hearing opposition.

“Carney has called this legislation the most consequential legislation of this Parliament… then Parliament should take its time,” he said. “We should open the doors to hear from the full range of Canadians, from environmentalists to Indigenous people to labor groups to business groups to everybody who’s affected to make sure we get it right.”

Failing to do so opens a huge risk for the government that the stated aim of the bill – building big things faster – won’t be possible due to a lacking societal buy-in, potential court challenges, or protests, he said.

“That’s no way to govern, and I think it’ll backfire on the government,” Davies said.

Per the workplan MPs agreed to, any proposed amendments to Bill C-39 are due to the committee clerk by 5 p.m. ET on Nov. 4, with clause-by-clause consideration taking place mid-month.

CTV News asked Minister of the Environment, Climate Change and Nature Julie Dabrusin’s office for comment on both the specific scientific concerns and the reservations about the committee process.

In an emailed response, Dabrusin’s office reasserted that Bill C-39 will not compromise on environmental standards.

“The scope of environmental assessments remains the same and will continue to consider a broad set of factors, including environmental, health and social effects, as well as Indigenous and traditional knowledge. Any project will continue to be subject to legally-binding conditions and mitigation measures,” said her press secretary Amy Falkner.

Falkner also said that the government has been open to receiving public feedback about the legislation “and are committed to doing so as bill C-39 moves through Parliament.”

items.title: Canada Post CEO touts ‘early signs’ of recovery even as financial woes persist
items.description: The head of Canada Post says it is showing “early signs” of financial recovery despite falling revenue and bigger losses in the first half of the year.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Canada Post CEO Doug Ettinger poses in front of an electric delivery vehicle after a news conference on the postal service’s plans to transform their fleet of 14,000 vehicles, in Ottawa, on Thursday, June 9, 2022. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Justin Tang</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The head of Canada Post says it is showing “early signs” of financial recovery despite falling revenue and bigger losses in the first half of the year.
items.body:
Canada Post has begun to show “early signs” of financial recovery, its CEO says, as the beleaguered Crown corporation starts to step back from the fiscal cliff.

At its annual public meeting, Doug Ettinger said Canada Post is winning back some of the parcel delivery market that has slipped away since 2019. To make those gains, the Crown corporation is giving shipping discounts to small businesses and pushing a new direct-to-consumer online marketplace.

“I am extremely confident that the organization is not only trending in the right direction, it is poised to re-establish itself as a crucial infrastructure built to serve Canada,” Ettinger said, invoking national sovereignty to make the case for a healthy postal service.

  • Latest updates on company news here

However, its network of post offices remains “overbuilt” in cities and must be scaled down, he said Thursday. 

Ettinger qualified that Canada Post will continue to serve rural and remote communities. “We will not abandon the small communities that rely on us.”

Switching the remaining four million addresses that still enjoy doorstep delivery to community mailboxes within about five years marks a key pillar of Canada Post’s plan to overhaul its business model in the face of declining letter mail and financial losses.

The Crown corporation launched an online tool Thursday that lets customers with door-to-door delivery enter their postal code to see when their area is slated for conversion to a community mailbox. The first such switch in more than 10 years was completed a few days ago in Winnipeg and Sept-Îles, Que., executives said.

By the end of 2027, about 700,000 more households from Halifax to Victoria will be collecting their mail from the compact aluminum boxes, according to Canada Post.

In August, the organization reported losses of $277 million before taxes for the second quarter of the year, marking an improvement from $407 million pre-tax loss a year earlier.

The three-month period revealed “signs of an early turning point,” said chief financial officer Rindala El-Hage, as revenue rose — from parcels in particular — and operating costs plummeted.

“These results do not resolve our structural challenges, but they show that ... the trajectory can improve,” she said.

Ettinger twice referred to the “fiscal cliff” the service still faces and pointed the finger at successive governments for a sluggish response. “This is not where any of us wanted to be,” said the chief executive.

But Ettinger, who is slated to step down at the end of his second term in March, said the current government under Prime Minister Mark Carney has opened the door to overdue shifts, such as lifting the moratorium on new community mailboxes imposed by his predecessor in 2015.

Other reforms include weekend parcel delivery — under a staggered rollout across the country that kicked off this month — and expected post office closures.

To win over small businesses, they will continue to receive Canada Post’s biggest shipping discounts no matter how small the volume through the end of the year. A 15 per cent discount on fuel surcharges for domestic parcels eases the pain of price hikes tied to the soaring price of gas and diesel.

A new online marketplace dubbed Canada Shops is also in the testing phase. Launched over the summer, it aims to connect Canadian retailers with domestic shoppers.

Between 2019 and 2023, the postal service’s share of the parcel market plummeted to 29 per cent from 62 per cent, as Amazon and other competitors seized on skyrocketing demand for next-day deliveries.

“This isn’t about competing with other marketplace giants,” said chief marketing officer Rod Hart of the direct-to-consumer platform.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The update from Canada Post comes less than five months after postal workers approved a tentative agreement that will boost their wages nearly 10 per cent in the first 24 months of the five-year deal.

The green light given by most of the union’s 55,000 employees followed more than two years of labour strife. Greater use of community mailboxes, which reduce the need for letter carriers, was among the sticking points.

In December 2024, the federal government asked the Canada Industrial Relations Board to step in to quash a month-long strike, and struck an Industrial Inquiry Commission to find a path forward. That probe, led by William Kaplan, made a series of recommendations that were later adopted and rolled out in a suite of sweeping changes to Canada Post’s mandate.

Announced in September 2025, the overhaul lifted the community mailbox moratorium and ended the freeze on rural post office closures — some locations are now surrounded by suburban subdivisions — that had been in place since 1994, covering close to 4,000 outlets.

Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

items.body:
OTTAWA — The Conservatives are calling on the government to implement temporary resident exit tracking, boost collaboration with the provinces and further reduce permanent residency admissions in the coming immigration levels plan.

Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner outlined these and other demands in a press conference today, and blamed government policy for a rise in anti-immigrant sentiment in recent years.

She said the government should be putting more emphasis on integrating newcomers to restore faith in the system and ease social tensions around immigration.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday the government “will not budge” on its goal of making immigration numbers sustainable and its plan is “getting them to that level now.”

Last year’s immigration levels plan, which set a target of admitting 380,000 permanent residents annually between 2026 and 2028, also included two programs aimed at giving permanent status to more than 130,000 temporary residents who aren’t included in the broader target.

The government must provide an updated levels plan in the next few weeks.

items.title: Construction costs, policy certainty top B.C. builders' priorities ahead of B.C. election
items.description: Industry groups urge the next government to lower costs, improve transparency and strengthen coordination
items._ogDesc: Industry groups urge the next government to lower costs, improve transparency and strengthen coordination
items.body:
With the B.C. election approaching, builders across the province say they want the next government to address rising construction costs and provide greater policy consistency for the industry.

Improving the predictability of the project pipeline, transparency around how development fees are spent and communication among different levels of government are also among the priorities that building industry associations want the next government to address.

“Reducing the cost to build is felt right across the province,” said George Greenwood, CEO of the Canadian Home Builders' Association of BC (CHBA BC).

“The cost to acquire the land and then building materials, labour costs, these are all contributing to making homeownership more out of reach for average British Columbians.”

CHBA BC is calling for streamlining approval processes, reforms to the municipal infrastructure funding model and greater municipal transparency and accountability in how they calculate, collect and spend fees charged to developers.

The organization is also calling on the next government to pause potential mandatory changes to the province’s energy step codes, which set progressive energy-efficiency requirements for new construction in B.C. Greenwood argues it would add more costs to builders.

“We're just saying take a more stable approach, even putting it on a pause, let people catch their breath,” he said. “The economy is not strong right now. The housing market is not strong.”

The Vancouver Regional Construction Association (VRCA) is also urging the next government to look at ways to reduce charges imposed on developers and increase transparency on how the revenue is spent.

“The additional fees added to housing from development cost charges and other charges are not helping get housing built, not to mention all the other impacts of what's happening in the economy and interest rates,” said Jeannine Martin, president of VRCA.

“[We also want to see] more transparency on what's happening with that, what that's paying for, and how we are utilizing that to build housing.”

Chris Atchison, president of the BC Construction Association, said he also wants greater government transparency, including the reinstatement of the Major Projects Inventory reports, which was discontinued late last year.

Atchison said recent policy discussions, including a proposal to convert vacant condo units in designated growth areas into affordable homes using financing through Build Canada Homes and BC Housing, and a two per cent tax on vacant residential properties, have raised concerns about mixed policy signals to the construction industry.

“We need policy consistency and a predictable project pipeline. They're critical to housing delivery,” said Atchison.

“Because construction is a long-term industry, all of our projects can take years to plan, to finance, to approve and deliver, so businesses need confidence that the policy environment will remain stable throughout that process.”

Those who spoke with Business in Vancouver said they also hope to see better communication among different levels of government, saying there is still room for improvement, and continued investment in skilled trade training programs.

items.description: Keith Buchanan shares his views on Travelers, Aflac and Wells Fargo and the earnings potential of U.S. financial stocks.

items._ogDesc: Keith Buchanan shares his views on Travelers, Aflac and Wells Fargo and the earnings potential of U.S. financial stocks.
items.body:
The U.S. financial sector offers a window into business activity and consumer finances. Trading, initial public offerings, advisory work and credit trends help reveal the economy’s health.

BNN Bloomberg spoke with Keith Buchanan, senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments, about his three financial stock selections and how he evaluates opportunities across banking and insurance.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

Key Takeaways

  • Profitable underwriting and investment income support Travelers’ appeal as a source of relatively stable earnings, Buchanan said.
  • Travelers’ geographic reach helps diversify exposure to concentrated risks, including weather-related losses.
  • Aflac faces pressure from rising Japanese interest rates and a weaker yen, but Buchanan said those concerns have also helped improve its pricing environment.
  • Wells Fargo’s asset cap removal creates an opportunity to grow earnings and narrow its valuation gap with other major banks, provided it executes effectively.
  • A flattening yield curve and economic deterioration are key risks for financial stocks, particularly because of their potential effect on traditional bank lending profitability.

Read the full transcript below:

LINDSAY: It’s time now for Hot Picks, and our next guest has three financial companies on his radar. Let’s welcome in Keith Buchanan, senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments. Great to have you join us once again. Thank you.

LINDSAY: So, before we get into your actual picks, I always like to start with a broader look at the financial—at the sector. And this—today we’re talking about financials. What do you think is driving the financial sector right now? Is it one thing? Is it interest rates, earnings growth, the broader economy? Is it a number of things?

KEITH: I choose all the above. I think the financials is a unique space that really gives a glimpse into the window of many facets for our economy. We’ve seen interest rate volatility, trading, some anxiety among investors, also the IPO movement, and also the advisory businesses all really come together to kind of give a glimpse of business America and how small and midsize business are performing, but also some of the consumer elements, too, with credit cards and that, you know, some of the credit issues that—that are starting to bubble up here at the larger banks. We get a full view of—of the broader economy, which is interesting in covering the group on a day-to-day basis.

LINDSAY: Okay, so let’s get into your picks, then. The first one is Travelers. I know this—this company just also reported earnings. So tell us more about the opportunities you see—you see right now.

KEITH: Sure, Travelers is a company that really just is executing in a very high clip, not only from a, you know, writing profitable business, but also investment portfolios kicking in extra earnings that kind of just put the ice meal on the cake. The insurance business right now is one that—that gets left behind in moments like we’ve seen over the last couple of years. But in moments like we are right now, where there are several risks that investors are becoming more and more concerned about, the market really looks at some of these names as a very stable provider of earnings, which we think earnings will be kind of the balance of whether this market holds up over the next 12 to 18 months or whether there’s a bear market that ensues. And names like this will be more attractive the more the latter becomes a fear of the broader market. So Travelers is a name that we really feel like offers a lot to our clients’ portfolios right now.

LINDSAY: And it delivered a really strong third quarter. Like, what do you think was behind that performance?

KEITH: Again, just growing a profitable business. They—they’ve been able to move in P&C and property and casualty in a way that most smaller corporations haven’t been able to. They’re broader geographically, so they have been able to diversify from a lot of just really concentrated risks, whether it’s weather-related or otherwise. So, being bigger has been better, and they’ve been able to really execute it on an underwriting standpoint.

LINDSAY: Okay, Aflac, your next company for today, your next pick. Tell us more about this one.

KEITH: Sure, Aflac is a little different from Travelers. It doesn’t have, like, the best-of-breed allure to it. It has a, you know, of course, a big part of its business is in Japan, so we have to understand how currency really affects from a couple of different standpoints. But they’ve been executing a really more of a self-help story within the insurance space, smaller and, of course, you know, a different facet of the business. But, you know, Aflac has been able to perform extremely well from a stock standpoint, and we’re really—again, it really—we really appreciate what it offers our strategy going forward. For specifically within the financial space, where it’s really hard to find these more stable earnings growers without concerns about the economy declines over the next couple of years.

LINDSAY: Well, because Japan is one of Aflac’s biggest markets, right? Like, are they facing any pressure from the rising interest rates and a weaker yen?

KEITH: Yes, they are, but in an interesting, kind of ironic way, the fear that kind of comes up from that actually drives, from a pricing standpoint, better pricing environment in Japan. So that—that’s kind of helped them in a—in a really ironic twist of fate. So we really, from aspect of what it offers their business lines, you know, exposure to Japan is something we actually become to enjoy in these—again, some of these moments where we have a little more fear permeating the marketplace.

LINDSAY: Okay, your last pick for today is Wells Fargo. Tell us more about that.

KEITH: Again, another self-help story, but more on the major bank side. Without the asset cap now, they really have opened the door, and execution is the way they kind of drive value through that door. You get it at a discount that, frankly, has been warranted over the last several years. We feel like it might be a way to really drive shareholder value going forward. The earnings picture is much more clear now, and we feel like Wells has a diversification among its businesses and its geographies in order to drive that value going forward and close that valuation gap between Wells Fargo and the rest of the major banks. We feel like it’s a self-help story that’s earnings-driven and really has upside from here.

LINDSAY: I just want to go back to the general sector as well. Like, what’s the biggest risk—risk do you think financial stocks maybe face over the next even year or so?

KEITH: Sure. The biggest risk is a flattening yield curve that is—brings along the economic strain that a more distressed economy, even a recession, is among the more likely options. That’s not really baked in right now, but with the banks having so much market cap, the insurers and those names believe are having a market cap to continue to drive the space higher. That is the scenario that we’re going to in the 20—later 2027, maybe even 2028. So economic decline is obviously the risk there, and also, you know, a more flattening yield curve makes that—that book of business or the big banks and traditional lending business much more difficult to become profitable. So those are the concerns we have with the space going forward.

LINDSAY: Okay, we got to leave it there. Keith Buchanan, senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments. Great to have you join us. Thank you.

items.description: Industry Minister Melanie Joly has given Stelco 15 days to make good on its agreements with the Canadian government or face legal action.

items._ogDesc: Industry Minister Melanie Joly has given Stelco 15 days to make good on its agreements with the Canadian government or face legal action.
items.body:
Industry Minister Melanie Joly has given Stelco’s U.S. owner 15 days to make good on commitments it made when purchasing the plant or face legal action.

Joly made the demand in a letter to Stelco’s general counsel on Thursday. In an accompanying statement on X, she wrote that Cleveland-Cliffs, the American company that acquired the steel producer in 2024, made legally binding agreements that were key to allowing the transaction to move forward.

“As we stand right now, the business is still taking steps to lay off 500 workers. Despite being given multiple opportunities, Cleveland-Cliffs has repeatedly failed to demonstrate that they are compliant with their undertakings. That is unacceptable.”

CTV News reached out to Cleveland-Cliffs, which opted not to comment.

CEO endorsed tariffs, says Joly

Last month, Cleveland-Cliffs announced it would shut down part of its Ontario operations, across the Hamilton and Lake Erie facilities, axing up to 500 jobs.

At the time, the company cited low steel prices and tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump.

The Trump Administration has used Section 232 of the American Trade Expansion Act to impose tariffs on steel and aluminum imports, amounting to as much as 50 per cent.

Canada exported US$4.6 billion-worth of steel into the U.S. last year, far less than the US$7 billion in 2024, prior to the expanded tariffs.

The letter contends that Cleveland-Cliffs submitted a number of formal “undertakings” under the Investment Canada Act. Among those, it pledged to be a “strong advocate for policies that benefit both the U.S. and Canadian steel industries.”

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Joly’s letter argues Cliffs’ chief executive officer, Lourenco Goncalves, has advocated in favour of U.S. tariffs affecting Canadian steel, and “publicly asserted that he influenced those tariffs.”

For example, she wrote, “On Jan. 14, 2026, Mr. Goncalves testified before the Congressional Steel Caucus of the United States Congress. In his prepared remarks, Mr. Goncalves expressly and repeatedly endorsed the imposition of Section 232 tariffs against Canada.

“He took credit for blocking Stelco from selling steel into the U.S. market. He stated that the increase in Section 232 tariffs to 50 per cent was ‘absolutely necessary.’ In his testimony, he called Canada a ‘bad player[s]’ and a ‘steel dumping machine’ and likened it to China and Brazil.”

Joly’s letter also claims Cliffs was the first signatory on an industry memo sent to Trump on Jan. 28 advocating for steel levies.

In October, Stelco requested relief from some of its commitments due to “unprecedented and escalating disruptions” facing the industry, according to Joly’s letter. The company requested relief from its commitments on employment to be reduced.

Days later, a union president confirmed 90 members received layoff notices on Oct. 5, and that 85 members expected to receive notices by the end of the following week.

A drawn-out battle?

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles, speaking at Queen’s Park in Toronto on Thursday, said Stelco workers are concerned about the prospect of “this becoming a very long legal battle.”

While that may be a necessary step to protect jobs in Hamilton, she added, near-term relief for laid-off workers must be a part of the government’s response.

“What is the government going to do to ensure that they are OK? That their families are taken care of?” asked Stiles.

Conservative MP Michael Guglielmin, that party’s senior advisor on steel policy, took issue with what he called “shifting” timelines.

What our workers need today is concrete action,” he said. “Six days ago, Minister Joly had said that we’re only days away from resolving the issue with Stelco and the Stelco workers,” he said in Ottawa. “Today we hear they have 15 days to rehire the workers. ... What our workers need today is concrete action.”

Asked about timelines, Joly said the letter is an important part of a legal process to present and detail evidence ahead of a potential court challenge.

items._ogDesc: Canadian mortgage credit growth posted its weakest August since 2013. BMO warns renewed rate hikes could add pressure to borrowers.
items.body:
Canadian borrowing is losing steam just as interest rate hikes come back into focus. Bank of Canada (BoC) data shows mortgage credit posted its smallest August increase since 2013, pushing annual growth to a pace rarely seen outside housing corrections. With nearly a third of new mortgages carrying variable rates, renewed tightening could further throttle slow activity.

Canadian Mortgage Debt Growth Slows To Weakest August Since 2013

Canadian household debt: Residential mortgage credit, annual growth rate.

Source: Bank of Canada; Better Dwelling.

Residential mortgage debt advanced 0.3% (+$7.1 billion) to $2.45 trillion in August. That was unusually slow, marking the smallest August increase since 2013. Annual growth decelerated for a tenth straight month, leaving the balance only 3.8% (+$89.1 billion) higher than last year. It’s a slump that’s catching the attention of at least one Big Six economist.

“In August, household mortgage debt grew just 3.8% y/y, the slowest pace since the worst of the housing correction in 2023-24 (and before that, since the early 2000s),” explained Shelly Kaushik, senior economist at BMO Capital Markets.

Ontario & BC Slump, Weak New Condo Demand Slows Growth

The weak credit growth serves as a reminder that market stabilization isn’t the same as normalization. While the national market is stabilizing, it’s masking the prolonged slump in BC and Ontario. Weak demand in these regions, along with weak new condo demand in general, “has kept a lid on the recent recovery in borrowing,” according to Kaushik.

The data highlights another area the Bank of Canada (BoC) may be watching, explains Kaushik. “Canadian monthly credit aggregates, which typically fly under the radar, highlighted an ongoing slowdown in the economy’s most interest-rate-sensitive sector just as the Bank of Canada may be looking more closely at raising rates.”

Rate Hikes May Add To Mortgage Payment Stress

Bond yields are surging higher, but housing demand remains relatively weak. “Suffice it to say the housing market isn’t exactly in need of extinguishing,” says Kaushik. Variable-rate loans accounted for roughly 30% of new mortgages in Q2, according to BoC data cited by BMO, leaving those borrowers exposed to renewed rate hikes.

“Indeed, a new tightening cycle could add payment stress to variable rate mortgage holders,” she warns. Mortgage borrowing is already struggling to regain momentum. Renewed tightening could add further pressure to both the recovery and the households carrying that debt.

items.title: FINTRAC at two years: what brokers are still getting wrong
items.description: Glasslake Funding’s Doug Robinson: FINTRAC non-compliance is a risk brokers can no longer ignore
items.content: <p>Glasslake Funding’s Doug Robinson: FINTRAC non-compliance is a risk brokers can no longer ignore</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282884379552081.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Glasslake Funding’s Doug Robinson: FINTRAC non-compliance is a risk brokers can no longer ignore
items.body:
With additional reporting by Fergal McAlinden

Two years after mortgage brokers became reporting entities under Canada’s anti-money laundering framework, a senior industry voice is sounding a warning: the window for wilful inaction has closed.

Doug Robinson of Glasslake Funding, a Toronto-based alternative mortgage lender, drew on a dual background in policing and lending to take stock of where brokerages stand on compliance.

Robinson was speaking at the Mortgage Professionals Canada conference in Calgary, two years on from October 11, 2024, the date on which the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) brought mortgage administrators, brokers and lenders under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA).

“I can pretty much guarantee this will not blow over,” Robinson said.

“If you’re a broker or owning a brokerage and you haven’t done any work on FINTRAC stuff, you may want to.”

Robinson described two camps that emerged when the rules were first announced: those who hired compliance staff, documented policies and prepared in earnest, and those who hoped the requirements might quietly disappear.

As the debate over challenging FINTRAC requirements for brokers rumbles into 2026, Robinson argued the regulator’s baseline expectations are more achievable than commonly assumed.

“FINTRAC doesn’t want mortgage brokers to become experts in reporting money launderers,” he said.

“They just wanted to add mortgage brokers because you guys are governed by a regulator and you have an obligation, and it fortifies Canada’s anti-money laundering landscape.”

Know your client — or know the risk

Robinson anchored his anti-money laundering (AML) framework around three questions every broker must be able to answer: who is the applicant, how will they service the mortgage, and where did the down payment come from? The third, he said, is the most exploited vulnerability in the transaction chain.

“In lending and in mortgages, the down payment is usually, in my opinion, the softest spot,” Robinson said.

“If someone’s looking to get a whole bunch of money into the system in one spot, they’ll usually do it through down payment.”

He urged brokers to build what he called “reasonability statements” — documented explanations that account for the origin of funds — warning that gift letters alone carry limited evidentiary weight.

“The reasonability statements go a long way,” he said. 

Policies, risk ratings, and a lender blind spot

Robinson outlined five elements every brokerage should have in place:

  1. a designated compliance officer or administrator
  2. written policies
  3. a company-level risk assessment
  4. AML training — leverageable through MPC for smaller shops
  5. a completed two-year self-assessment

 A smaller brokerage, he noted, can assign compliance responsibilities to an administrative staff member, provided the function is kept separate from the sales side.

His sharpest criticism was aimed at lenders. “In my opinion, lenders are soft on being concerned about where the repayment comes from,” Robinson said.

Accelerated or lump-sum payments made after funding, he argued, too often pass without scrutiny, a gap that sophisticated money laundering schemes are positioned to exploit.

Robinson also flagged British Columbia’s unexplained wealth orders (UWOs), a civil mechanism under the province’s Civil Forfeiture Act that can compel individuals to account for assets exceeding $75,000 that appear disproportionate to their known income, all without requiring a criminal conviction.

Some mortgage professionals argue that regulation is both burdensome and necessary. Robinson, a former police officer, sits firmly in the latter camp. He suggested the UWO model could spread beyond British Columbia as the courts test its constitutional limits.

“There’s no downside to reporting an unusual transaction report to FINTRAC,” he said.

“Sometimes big investigations start from a really small report that someone put in sometime.”

items._ogDesc: GTA new home sales rose in September but remain historically weak. Single-family prices plunged $180k in four months, while condo sales hit a record low.
items.body:
Greater Toronto Area (GTA) new home sales picked up in September, but the recovery remains shaky. BILD and Altus Group data shows sales rose 63.9% from last year, but they remain historically weak. The bigger story is prices—nearly a third of the single-family correction has occurred in the past 4 months. New condo prices have held up better, but buyers are balking with sales hitting a record low for the segment.

Toronto New Single-Family Homes Fell $180k In The Past 4 Months

The Altus Group benchmark price of single-family and condo apartment homes across Greater Toronto.

Source: Altus Group; BILD GTA.

New home prices continued to slide, led by single-family homes. The segment’s benchmark slipped 0.2% (-$2.1k) to $1.25 million in September, down 13.3% (-$190.7k) from last year. September’s decline was modest, but the bigger story is the sudden return of plunging prices.

Prices have effectively fallen off a cliff since May, dropping 12.7% (-$180.8k) in just four months. That accounts for nearly 95% of the decline over the past year. The benchmark is now 35.5% (-$687.1k) below its July 2022 record high. The percentage decline over the past four months alone is more than a third of the total decline from the peak, leaving prices where they were almost 6 years ago.

New condo prices have held up much better. The segment’s benchmark fell 1.0% (-$10.3k) to $1.03 million in September, just 0.2% (-$1.7k) below last year. Prices are now 17.6% (-$220.9k) below the March 2022 record high—roughly half the percentage decline seen in single-family homes. That relative strength has narrowed the price gap between the two segments to just $215.2k. Whether that means single-family homes are now relatively weak or new condos are set to correct further is anyone’s guess. However, a breakdown of home sales suggests demand for new condos at these prices is almost non-existent.

New Home Sales Rise, But New Condo Sales Hit A September Low

Greater Toronto new home sales in September.

Source: Altus Group; BildGTA; Better Dwelling.

New home sales jumped, but the above chart should temper expectations. There were 949 units sold in September, up 63.9% from last year. Single-family homes accounted for 820 sales, the strongest September since 2021. Condos weren’t so lucky: just 129 units sold, down 40.3% from last year and the weakest September on record.

The increase is welcome, but a base effect makes it sound more impressive than reality. Despite the jump, total sales remained 52% below the 10-year September average. Sales of single-family homes have recovered, while condo demand continues to find new lows.

New Home Inventory Falls, But Remains Elevated

New home inventory fell but remains lofty by the region’s historical standards. There were 19,957 new homes for sale in September, down 8.2% from last year. Despite falling below the past two years, inventory remains at its third-highest September level since 2015. New home inventory might be lighter, but relative to sales, this remains a weak demand balance.

Toronto’s new home sales improved, but the numbers are less impressive when broken down. Single-family sales picked up alongside steep declines in prices. As for condos, prices are firmer, but with sales at record lows, buyers are balking at those prices. Last month’s numbers are even less impressive when one considers it’s the result of billions in bailout programs. From developer bailouts to tax incentives, that’s a lot of public support for a market struggling to find buyers.

items.title: Slower homebuilding risks wiping out Canada’s affordability gains, economists warn
items.description: The national housing market may be sluggish, but the lacklustre pace of housing construction could worsen affordability problems
items.content: <p>The national housing market may be sluggish, but the lacklustre pace of housing construction could worsen affordability problems</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639282861144967017.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The national housing market may be sluggish, but the lacklustre pace of housing construction could worsen affordability problems
items.body:
Canada’s housing market has been mired in a years-long slump, pushing prices lower amid plunging demand – but economists still say the sluggish pace of homebuilding could worsen the affordability crisis in the long run.

Mathieu Laberge (pictured top), chief economist and senior vice president at Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) and Stéfane Marion, chief economist and strategist at National Bank of Canada, sounded an ominous note on the construction outlook during speeches at the recent Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) National conference in Calgary.

Laberge highlighted how the slower pace of construction in 2026 could have significant negative consequences for the market down the line.

“Our latest housing supply report points to the central issue: right here, right now across Canada, construction is slowing faster than the underlying need for housing,” he said. “If we react to a softer market by stopping too much construction, we may be protecting ourselves from today’s risks – but we’re also creating tomorrow’s shortages.

“We are at a very high risk that by not providing the appropriate and sufficient supply today, we will lose the improvement in affordability we’ve seen two or three, or five years down the road.”

Residential construction continues to slide

The Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) recently revised its home price growth forecast downward for the year, basing that adjustment on waning purchase demand because of wider economic uncertainty and rising interest rates.

Construction in certain sectors is grinding to a halt against that backdrop. Marion noted that a sizable portion of recently-built condos has not been absorbed, marking the highest proportion seen since the early 1990s – and the resulting homebuilding slowdown has been stark.

Laberge said just six companies of more than 500 employees currently build residential homes across the country, and the sector is also being left behind in the new digital era. In a recent McKinsey study of the level of digitization across industries, construction came second last, he pointed out – only ahead of hunting and agriculture.

Canada building the wrong home types, says Laberge

It’s also often pointed out that the type of home construction currently being prioritized is missing the mark. Condominium construction, particularly in Toronto and Vancouver, has dominated homebuilding in recent decades – leaving a surplus of smaller condos rather than family-sized homes.

“Canada doesn’t simply have too much or too little housing,” Laberge said. “The reality is that we have a mismatch between the homes people need and the homes the system is producing. What’s small is unaffordable and what’s large is unavailable.

“This is the supply families need and they are seeking desperately, and they cannot find it right now.”

What’s more, the homebuying lull isn’t destined to last forever, and a ramping-up of purchase activity could put even further strain on national housing supply if construction doesn’t gather pace.

“It takes, give or take, six to eight years to deliver a big housing unit, whether it’s condo or rental, in any of the larger centres across Canada. Demand can shift on a dime,” Laberge cautioned.

“Young adults living with parents, people sharing homes longer than they plan, newcomers settling permanently, and families delaying their next move can all come back into the market when confidence returns. And that will return at some point. This is not a one-year story. This is a pent-up demand story that will play out over the next three, four, five years.”

For now, there seems little prospect of homebuilding accelerating to meet the required annual level – particularly with more than a million extra workers in the construction industry needed, according to Marion, to satisfy demand.

Laberge said it makes no sense to ease off on construction even in a quieter market because it will ultimately have a negative effect on the affordability outlook. “We should not close a fire station because it’s raining,” he said. “We should welcome the rain but not sell the truck.”

items.content: <p>New Wahi analysis finds four-bedroom GTA condos up while studio sales nearly vanish</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282832912037174.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: New Wahi analysis finds four-bedroom GTA condos up while studio sales nearly vanish
items.body:
The Greater Toronto Area’s condominium market is fracturing along size lines. New research from Wahi, a Toronto-based digital real estate platform and brokerage, finds that buyers who acquired larger units at the outset of the pandemic are still holding gains, while the one-bedroom segment has dropped 14% from Q1 2020 and has recorded flat or negative pricing in every consecutive quarter since Q1 2022.

The analysis compares median sale prices and transaction volumes across condominium types between Q1 2020 and Q1 2026, adding texture to a correction that Canadian mortgage professionals have followed closely.

Wahi’s tracking of GTA days on market through the first half of 2026 showed condominiums averaging 36 days to find a buyer in Q2 2026, roughly three to four times longer than during the market’s 2022 peak. 

Small units feel the weight of investor retreat

The data is most acute at the bottom of the size ladder. In Q1, the median price of a one-bedroom Greater Toronto Area condominium was $480,000, with 1,574 units changing hands. That's down 39% from Q1 2020 and 66% below the peak recorded in Q1 2021.

Studios have fared even worse. Just seven transactions were recorded in the first quarter of 2026, against a high of 230 in Q1 2022.

“In today’s GTA condo market, the end user is the main source of anything resembling demand,” said Ryan McLaughlin, economist at Wahi.

“There simply isn’t much appetite among buyers for smaller units, which have historically been geared primarily towards investors looking to flip them and/or rent them out.”

The broker community has had a front-row seat to the fallout. Christine Xu, founder of Money Broker Canada and a 26-year industry veteran, described the pre-construction investor collapse starkly when speaking at MortgageFest Canada 2026.

“A lot of those people are racing masters — they invest in a whole bunch of pre-construction condos and they are being hit the most. Big shot realtors who bought so many pre-construction condos and now — bankruptcy. We see bankruptcy all over the place,” she said.

On pricing, Xu was equally direct: “The price is almost 50% of the original purchase price. So the original owner walked away, gave the condo back to the builder.”

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada, says Ottawa should allow foreign buyers to purchase new-build homes, pointing to unsold condo inventory and the government's goal of making Canada more attractive to investors. https://t.co/hUVWtFthRu — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 20, 2026

Larger units offer a buffer — for now

Further up the size spectrum, the picture is more resilient, though still far from comfortable. Two-bedroom condominiums recorded a Q1 2026 median of $630,000, just 2% above Q1 2020 levels.

Three-bedroom units reached $700,000 — a 13% gain — while four-plus-bedroom condos led all categories at $715,000, up 15% over the six-year study period.

Transaction volumes have not been spared regardless of size: two-bedroom sales fell 35% from Q1 2020, three-bedroom activity dropped 43%, and four-plus-bedroom transactions declined 33%.

“Although this is likely not the kind of appreciation condo owners are hoping for, these numbers demonstrate something important about the GTA real estate market in general,” McLaughlin said.

“Even in the harshest environment in decades, buyers who purchase the right type of unit and are able to hold on for the longer term are insulated from the worst effects of a correction.”

“What’s striking is these units have maintained pricing even as sales volumes have collapsed across the board,” he added.

“However, it seems that buyers of larger three- and four-bedroom units have less room for price negotiation.”

For end users — the segment McLaughlin identifies as the market’s only real source of demand — the window may be more open than headlines suggest.

Reaza Ali, national business development manager at Heartwood Financial Group, told MortgageFest Canada 2026, “The market has come into a position now, that those with resources, it’s a fantastic opportunity to jump in... I would focus in on is the affordability piece there, because the price points on these properties are more in line with where they should have been.”

items.description: Tru Cooperative Bank CEO says proportionate rules are key to boosting banking competition in Canada
items.content: <p>Tru Cooperative Bank CEO says proportionate rules are key to boosting banking competition in Canada</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282819062614560.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Tru Cooperative Bank CEO says proportionate rules are key to boosting banking competition in Canada
items.body:
Canada’s newest federal credit union is calling on Ottawa to overhaul its merger and regulatory framework, warning that without meaningful reform, smaller institutions cannot build national scale and Canadians will be left with a banking market dominated by a handful of major lenders.

In an opinion piece published in The Hill Times, Launi Skinner, CEO of Tru Cooperative Bank in Langley, British Columbia, outlined three priorities for the federal government:

  1. clearer merger regulations and appropriate tax treatment
  2. coordinated review processes across federal agencies
  3. capital requirements calibrated to an institution’s actual size and risk profile

“For far too long, Canadians have had limited choice when it comes to national banking options,” Skinner wrote.

Tru Cooperative Bank, formerly First West Credit Union, became federally regulated in April and currently serves approximately 290,000 members with approximately $21 billion in total assets and assets under administration.

In September, it announced a proposed merger with Ontario’s Libro Credit Union that would create an organization serving approximately 470,000 members with nearly $33 billion in combined assets, subject to member and regulatory approvals.

The case for a stronger middle tier

Canada’s national residential mortgage market carries more than $2.4 trillion in outstanding debt, according to Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) data for December 2025, yet most credit unions remain regionally concentrated.

“Canada needs more institutions between those two ends of the market,” Skinner wrote — cooperatives with national capabilities and the local accountability that distinguishes them from publicly traded banks.

The appetite to fill that gap is already visible at the lender level. At MortgageFest Canada 2026, Bekim Merdita, head of sales and marketing at QuestBank, formerly Community Trust, described the institution’s positioning. 

“Community Trust, 50-year-old trust company. And really, at the end of last year, we got our banking licence — a Schedule 1 bank — and rebranded ourselves to Quest Bank. It gives us the ability to not just do mortgage products, but other products as well that serve the consumer and really start building a financial ecosystem for our consumer.”

The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) has signalled a less conservative approach to approving new banking entrants, and the regulator’s updated approvals framework launched in June aims to widen market access further.

For brokers navigating a more complex lender roster, regulatory inconsistency is already a top frustration. Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer of WealthOne Bank of Canada, told MortgageFest Canada 2026. 

"The biggest pain points that we’re hearing from brokers is the ever-changing policies, the ever-changing rules, the ever-changing processes that lenders are doing," he said. 

"Every single week a lender has changed how you submit a deal, what forms you need, what documents — and brokers are struggling to keep up."

What Ottawa needs to do

Skinner argued that mergers involving federal credit unions — requiring review by OSFI, the Competition Bureau, and the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC), alongside the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC) and the Department of Finance — should not generate duplicative information requests or conflicting regulatory interpretations.

“No responsible cooperative leader is asking for weaker consumer protection or lower standards of safety and soundness,” she wrote.

“But equivalent standards do not always require identical requirements.”

She also called for proportionate capital rules, arguing requirements designed around systemically important banks divert management capacity away from cybersecurity, digital banking, and small-business lending at mid-sized cooperatives.

Federally regulated credit unions now hold approximately $47 billion of the $330 billion in total assets across Canadian credit unions nationally, according to the Canadian Credit Union Association (CCUA).

The Tru–Libro combination, if approved, would represent the sector’s most substantial attempt yet to fill the gap Skinner has identified, and the clearest test of whether Ottawa’s updated framework can deliver.

items.title: Amazon-Leased Ajax Facility Listed As Part Of 3-Building Industrial Portfolio
items.description:
Markets speak, and the commercial real estate market in the Greater Toronto Area is indicating that there is a demand for institutional-grade industrial properties, according to yet another new listing for a high-profile industrial property that came online this week.

After a TELUS-leased industrial property and a Tesla-leased industrial property were listed in recent weeks, this time around it is an industrial property leased to Amazon, among others.

The property is an industrial park consisting of three buildings located at 789 Salem Road North, 689 Salem Road North, and 210 Kerrison Drive East in Ajax. The three properties span a total of 107 acres along Salem Road North between Rossland Road East and Kerrison Drive East.

789 Salem Road North spans 58.2 acres, was constructed in 2021, and is home to 1,080,710 sq. ft of space that is 100% leased to tech giant Amazon.

689 Salem Road North spans 9.7 acres, was constructed in 2023, and is home to 181,281 sq. ft of space that is 100% leased to wholesale company All-Special and panel manufacturer SkyRise Prefab Building Solutions.

Lastly, 210 Kerrison Drive East spans 39.1 acres, was constructed in 2022, and is home to 716,548 sq. ft of space that is 100% leased to clothing company H&M.

The properties are owned by CPSP Ajax Nominee Inc. — a joint venture between investment firm Crestpoint Real Estate Investments and pension fund PSP Investments — and belong to the GTA East Industrial Park originally developed by Crestpoint, Broccolini, and Blackwood Partners.

The Listing

Earlier this month, 789 Salem Road North, 689 Salem Road North, and 210 Kerrison Drive East were together listed for sale by Reid Taylor, Lucas Atkins, Matthew Thrift, Connor Molony, Graham Meader, Colin Alves, Luke Dawson, and Edward Plumley of Colliers on an unpriced basis.

  • Address: 789 Salem Road North, 689 Salem Road North, and 210 Kerrison Drive East, Ajax
  • Year Built: 2021 / 2023 / 2022
  • Site Area: 107.0 acres
  • Gross Leasable Area: 1,978,539 sq. ft
  • Current Occupancy Rate: 100%
  • Price: Unpriced
  • Listed By: Colliers (Reid Taylor, Lucas Atkins, Matthew Thrift, Connor Molony, Graham Meader, Colin Alves, Luke Dawson, and Edward Plumley)

According to Colliers, the buildings are equipped with “state-of-the-art” shipping and receiving infrastructure, 40-ft clear heights, and large-format functional warehouse configurations. The properties also include a total of 227 truck-level shipping doors, 363 trailer parking stalls, and 1,160 dedicated vehicle stalls.

The tenancies have a weighted average lease term of 6.8 years, and Colliers says the tenants have made significant capital investments in their spaces. Amazon’s facility was purpose-built for them, H&M’s facility includes an automated conveyor system, and All-Special’s space includes modular cold storage installations.

“At 1.98 million sf, the Portfolio represents approximately 4% of GTA East’s total industrial inventory,” said Colliers in a listing brochure obtained by STOREYS. “Limited near-term power availability in Durham Region makes future development in the immediate area challenging, rendering this scale of product difficult to replicate. The Portfolio is well-positioned to capitalize on sustained demand within Canada’s most critical and supply-constrained industrial market.”

There’s also the location, which is approximately 2 km from Highway 401, provides access to Highway 407 and 412, and is within a 35-minute drive of downtown Toronto. The assets also benefit from the state of the industrial market.

“Greater Toronto is one of North America’s top-performing industrial markets, with a current vacancy rate of 2.2%,” added Colliers. “Demand is supported by a growing consumer base and continued investment in domestic supply chains, while land scarcity and elevated development costs constrain new supply. This offering provides global investors with a valuable long-term land position and immediate scale in one of Canada’s most sought-after industrial markets.”

items.title: GTA High-Rise Sales Sink To A September Record Low
items.description:
Builders in the Greater Toronto Area sold 820 new low-rise homes in September, 17% above the 10-year average for the month. It’s the sixth month in a row low-rise sales have cleared that bar, which covers every month since the HST rebate program launched.

High-rise went the other way. Just 129 new high-rise units sold in September, according to new figures from the Building Industry and Land Development Association (BILD) and Altus Group, BILD’s official source for new home market data. That’s the lowest September on record for the segment, down 40% from September 2025 and 90% below the 10-year average. (BILD’s high-rise category includes units in low-, medium- and high-rise buildings, plus stacked townhouses.)

The low-rise surge isn’t enough to carry the market on its own. Total new home sales came to 949 in September. That’s up significantly from a year ago, and still 52% below the 10-year average of 1,978 units for the month.

Both segments are operating under the same program. BILD and Altus point to its rules around construction start and completion dates as the main obstacle keeping high-rise from taking part the way low-rise has. Altus also names a second problem.

“The high-rise sector remained plagued by undesirable inventory and program constraints centred on unattainable construction timelines,” said Edward Jegg, Research Manager at Altus Group.

High-rise inventory inched up to 12,909 units in September, or roughly 49 months of supply based on average sales over the last 12 months. Low-rise inventory sits at 7,048 homes, or 11 months’ worth.

And within low-rise, buyers are reaching for different product types than they used to.

“In the low-rise market, we have seen a positive response to the HST rebate program with increased sales activity and greater interest in semi-detached homes and townhouses,” said Justin Sherwood, Chief Operating Officer at BILD. “More than half of September’s sales were in semis and townhomes, representing a shift from traditional levels.”

Pricing has moved on that side of the market, too. The benchmark price for a new low-rise home was $1,246,764 in September, down 13.3% over the last 12 months. The high-rise benchmark held at $1,031,574, unchanged from a year ago. Both are gross prices that don’t reflect the HST rebate, so buyers who qualify would see an additional benefit.

Sherwood said the September high-rise numbers show the program rules need to change.

“The high-rise sales performance in September should be a wake-up call that there needs to be further measures and a modification of the program rules to allow the high-rise sector to better participate in the program, which would enable homebuyers in every segment of the housing market to benefit,” he said.

In Simcoe County, the split was starker still: 73 new low-rise homes sold in September at a weighted average price of $998,787, and not a single high-rise unit.
