items.body:
The Canadian Real Estate Association has downgraded its forecast for home sales activity in 2026 for the third straight quarter.

CREA now expects a total of 444,530 homes to be sold by the end of this year, representing a 5.2 per cent decrease from 2025.

That's down from its July forecast of a 1.4 per cent year-over-year decline, which marked a reversal from its April forecast of a one per cent gain. The association had predicted 5.1 per cent growth year-over-year in January.

CREA also projects the national average home price to tick 0.2 per cent higher on an annual basis to $681,681 this year, which is around $5,000 lower than predicted in the summer.

The association said its revised forecast comes amid a "roller-coaster year," with the global energy crisis fuelling inflation risks and affecting borrowing costs.

It cited higher fixed mortgage rates and ongoing uncertainty around variable rates, adding that the Bank of Canada has adopted "a notably more hawkish tone." Those factors hurt September's residential real estate activity, CREA said.

National home sales were down 7.7 per cent compared with the same month last year, while activity also fell 2.3 per cent from August.

“After a four-month run of modestly positive progress on demand, supply, and prices, many of Canada’s housing markets took a step back in September," said CREA senior economist Shaun Cathcart in a news release.

"This was hardly surprising given the latest jump in fixed mortgage rates, and with the Bank of Canada now widely expected to follow with a rate hike before the end of the year."

Worries about higher borrowing costs on the horizon led to a "significantly" shorter fall market compared to usual expectations for the season, said Marco Pedri, a broker with Shoreline Realty.

He said many of those considering a home purchase already made their move in the summer or first few weeks of fall "in an effort to lock in a favourable interest rate."

That's left remaining sellers in limbo, and they'll likely have to wait until next year before demand picks up again.

"It's honestly a game of chicken. It's about who's going to cave first," Pedri said.

"I think lot of purchasers ... are going to try and see what best deal they can get come January, February, March, when these sellers who have had their property on the record for so long may be at a point to just say, 'Hey, listen, at this point, I just want to sell.'"

In September, the national average sale price fell 1.6 per cent compared with the same month a year earlier to $666,538.

CREA’s own home price index, which aims to represent the sale of typical homes, edged 0.4 per cent lower from August to September, while the index dropped 3.4 per cent on a year-over-year basis.

The number of newly listed properties decreased 1.8 per cent month-over-month. Slightly more than 200,000 properties were listed for sale by the end of the month, up 1.8 per cent from a year earlier.

"While the Canada/U.S. trade war has recently escalated, and inflation concerns likely remain top-of-mind for Canadians, the rise in borrowing costs was probably the prime force behind September's monthly decline in home sales and average prices," said TD economist Rishi Sondhi in a note.

"Looking to 2027, we look for weak price growth across most regions next year, with loose supply/demand balances providing an additional drag on prices in B.C. and Ontario."

CREA said it now forecasts national home sales in 2027 to improve by 4.4 per cent to 464,235. The prediction bakes in slow but positive economic growth, the resumption of higher population growth, and more certainty for borrowers around the path for interest rates.

CREA said the latter should bring more pent-up demand into the market even with higher borrowing costs.

The national average home price is expected to rise 1.2 per cent from 2026 to $689,909 next year.

With housing affordability already stretched, Cathcart said "the big question going forward is how much farther will the (Bank of Canada) have to go to keep a lid on inflation next year?"

"Until that becomes clearer, this fresh round of uncertainty will likely send some buyers back to the sidelines," he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

items.title: Expert: Canada’s Homes Got Cheaper In September, But Buyers Still Pulled Back
items.description:
Canadian homes got cheaper in September. Buyers responded by purchasing fewer of them. A falling price is welcome, but it does little for a household whose mortgage approval no longer covers the home.

There were 36,657 residential sales in September, 7.7% fewer than a year earlier. Sales fell 2.3% from August after seasonal adjustment, so the decline went beyond the usual seasonal change.

September residential sales, not seasonally adjusted; the annual comparison uses CREA’s revised figures. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

The national benchmark price fell 0.4% during September and was 3.4% below a year earlier. The average sale price fell 1.6% annually to $666,538. The benchmark tracks comparable housing attributes; the average also changes with the mix of homes sold.

Annual changes in the unadjusted national MLS® HPI and average sale price. The average is affected by the mix of transactions. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

A discount can disappear into the mortgage

CREA blames the weaker outlook on another increase in fixed mortgage rates and uncertainty over how far variable rates may rise. Its October forecast points to renewed energy-related inflation risks and a more hawkish Bank of Canada. The assumption of an easy return to cheaper borrowing has become harder to defend.

A buyer can negotiate thousands off the purchase price and still face a payment they cannot carry. How much of the discount survives depends on the mortgage size, rate and amortization. The asking price has come down; the lender has not necessarily become more generous.

There is more scope to negotiate than there was during the boom, but national listings are hardly overflowing. CREA counted slightly more than 200,000 homes for sale at the end of September, up just 1.8% annually and close to the historical norm.

B.C.’s supply problem looks different from Manitoba’s

Canada had 4.9 months of inventory after seasonal adjustment. British Columbia had 7.0 months, Manitoba 2.4, and Saskatchewan 3.4. Ontario was at 4.7. The ratio compares the stock of listings with the current sales pace.

Seasonally adjusted residential months of inventory by province. Local property types can differ substantially. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

Ontario’s sales-to-new-listings ratio was only 41.9%, even with fewer months of inventory than B.C. The first ratio compares purchases with new listings arriving that month. Months of inventory compares the stock already available with the current sales pace.

A buyer shopping for an apartment can face much less competition than someone looking for a detached home in the same city. Provincial totals are a poor substitute for checking the homes that actually fit the budget.

Ontario is doing worse than the national forecast

CREA forecasts a 0.2% increase in the national annual average sale price to $681,681 in 2026. Ontario’s average is forecast to fall 3% to $809,334, and B.C.’s to fall 0.8%. Gains elsewhere keep the national number slightly positive.

Ontario and B.C. are the two provinces with forecast annual average-price declines in 2026. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

Newfoundland and Labrador has the strongest expected average-price growth this year at 5.7%, followed by Saskatchewan at 5%. CREA expects both to slow in 2027, to 3.1% and 2.5% respectively.

The national average is projected to reach $689,909 in 2027, up 1.2%. Ontario’s forecast gain is 0.7%, to $815,100. These are nominal annual averages. Ontario’s projected increase next year would recover only a small part of this year’s forecast loss.

Annual average transaction prices in Canadian dollars. Forecast values are not December price targets. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

Five years later, parts of Ontario are still cheaper

Greater Toronto’s September benchmark was 14.7% below its September 2021 level. Hamilton-Burlington was down 15.3%. Calgary was 24.6% higher, Quebec City 54.4% higher and St. John’s 41.2% higher. These are seasonally adjusted composite benchmarks measured from September 2021, before the 2022 peak.

Five-year changes in seasonally adjusted composite MLS® HPI benchmarks, September 2021 to September 2026. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

For an owner in one of the weaker Ontario markets, waiting has already failed to guarantee a better sale price. Moving can mean accepting less equity than expected while financing the next purchase at a higher rate. That is a good reason for a household to stay put, even when it would rather move.

Developers also have to compete with the prices buyers can pay for existing homes. Softer resale prices can squeeze the revenue available to cover a new project’s costs. CREA’s releases do not track presales, construction costs, or developer balance sheets, so they cannot tell us which projects will proceed.

Pent-up demand still needs a mortgage

CREA now expects 444,530 sales in 2026 and 464,235 in 2027. The forecast rebound of 4.4% would leave annual sales 4,436 below 2025. Even the recovery scenario falls short of that earlier year’s activity.

The confident pitch about pent-up demand has become harder to hear over repeated forecast cuts. CREA still uses the term in its 2027 outlook, but buyers are expected to return after economic growth, renewed population growth and a clearer interest-rate path help them along. Calling demand pent-up does not make it financeable.

That forecast also assumes limited further action by the Bank of Canada. September showed how quickly higher borrowing costs can interrupt a recovery. Buyers may get a better price this fall, but they still have to live with the payment.


CREA’s September 2026 monthly statistics and MLS® HPI package and October 2026 housing forecast, released October 16, 2026. Statistics retain the comparisons and revisions in the supplied media PDFs. Annual forecast prices are nominal transaction averages; forecasts are scenarios, not observed outcomes.

Monthly statistics: https://stats.crea.ca/en-ca/

Quarterly forecasts (October media PDF; July comparison uses the official July 15 vintage): https://www.crea.ca/housing-market-stats/canadian-housing-market-stats/quarterly-forecasts/

Charts: valery.ca · Data: CREA. MLS® and Multiple Listing Service® are CREA trademarks. Independent analysis; no CREA affiliation or endorsement.

items._ogDesc: Canadian bond yields are rising as hot US inflation is driving market expectations of four rate hikes from the Bank of Canada.
items.body:
The cross-border flow of goods is slow, but Canada’s imports of American inflation are ramping up. Government of Canada (GoC) short-term bond yields have climbed sharply since February. Gas prices were behind the initial surge, but yields are still climbing after gas stalled. A new report from BMO Capital Markets attributes the continued rise to hot U.S. inflation. The bank warns that markets are pricing in a full point of rate hikes from the Bank of Canada (BoC) by the end of 2027.

Canadian Bond Yields Pushed Higher By Hot U.S. Inflation

Higher gas prices have driven Canadian bond yields (and inflation) higher since February. BoC Governor Tiff Macklem warned yesterday that “every major central bank is worried…” because “…these costs have to go somewhere,” highlights BMO chief economist Douglas Porter.

Porter’s research shows the GoC 2-year bond yield’s correlation with gas prices at r=0.8, 1.0 being a perfect correlation. Gas prices and bond yields are moving very closely together, with the divergence only starting in September. Gas prices stabilized that month, but Canadian short- and medium-term yields rose further.

Porter flags the strong US jobs report as the catalyst that month. It was followed by a US Federal Reserve speech at Jackson Hole that was hawkish, suggesting the economy is running too hot. American inflation reported yesterday reinforced those concerns, as annual growth hit 3.7% in September, well above the 2% target.

Canadian yields are responding to that pressure, in addition to the energy bump. “Accordingly, the warm U.S. CPI has bumped Canadian yields again, with 2s backing up to 3.25%,” warns Porter.

Markets Expect Canadian Rates Will Rise 1 Point

Canada’s 2-year government bond yield hit 3.25% this week, reflecting expectations of tighter monetary policy. “That’s a full 100 bps above overnight rates, and the market is indeed expecting that much tightening by end-2027,” explains Porter.

The aggressive rise means higher mortgage rates may be ahead. A full point added to the overnight rate would trickle directly into variable rates. Fixed-rate mortgages are driven by bond yields, meaning they’re likely to lead here. BMO questions whether that much tightening is warranted while tariffs and trade uncertainty weigh on Canada. “That seems like a lot,” bluntly states Porter.

BMO Questions Scale of Tightening Amid Weak Economy

The market may be pricing in higher rates, but Canada’s economy may not be able to handle them. “Now, GoC yields are being largely pulled by domestic data—the weak jobs data helped pull them lower—and U.S. yields,” explains Porter.

Porter isn’t dismissing rate hikes, but suggests that market expectations are inflated. Higher rates would throttle demand, reducing inflation further. However, there’s still the matter of currency value that Porter doesn’t address. The situation the BoC faces is a little more complicated than just a demand issue.

Global commodities such as oil, wheat, and corn are generally priced in US dollars. That’s even the case for Canadian oil, which is priced based on global demand. Weak consumption can cool domestic price pressure, but a weaker loonie can still raise import costs. If hot US inflation keeps American rates elevated while Canadian weakness calls for relief, the BoC faces a difficult trade-off. A policy miss could deepen the slowdown or prolong inflation, raising stagflation risks.

items.title: Terra Bona’s Two-Tower Development Site In Markham Sold Under Receivership
items.description:
After being placed under receivership last December, the Grandview Tower project in Markham, Ontario has officially been sold, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court.

The project was set for 7115 Yonge Street plus 8, 10, 12, and 14 Grandview Avenue; a 0.95-acre site on the eastern side of Yonge Street between Meadowview Avenue and Grandview Avenue, about three blocks north of Centerpoint Mall.

The site consists of a vacant parcel of land and four single-family lots that Terra Bona Developments Ltd. was planning to redevelop. The original proposal was for a 36-storey condo tower with 443 units before it was later revised — following an appeal to the Ontario Land Tribunal — to one 49-storey tower and one 46-storey tower, with a grand total of 873 residential units.

For the project, Terra Bona — through Terrabona 7115 Yonge Ltd. — secured a first-ranking mortgage from Toronto-based Empirical Capital Corp. in October 2022 for the principal amount of $31,000,000, with interest accruing at the greater of 10.25% per annum or the RBC Prime Rate + 4.80%.

The loan was guaranteed by Majid Tavakoli and Majid Tavakoli Holdings Ltd.

According to loan documents filed in the proceeding, the purpose of the loan was to repay existing mortgages, fund a partner buy-out, and pay various fees. The existing mortgages that were taken out with the loan consisted of $15,777,261 owed to Forgestone Capital, and $4,311,000 owed to MarshallZehr.

The Receivership

According to court documents, Empirical Capital first initiated the receivership proceedings in November 2024 after Terra Bona defaulted on the loan when they failed to make an interest payment in May 2024.

Terra Bona then provided a proposal that would see them take out a second mortgage and make a significant paydown to Empirical in exchange for extending the maturity date of the loan from July 2024 to August 2025.

However, Empirical says Terra Bona was unable to secure that financing, and Empirical made a formal demand for payment in September 2024. The borrower was still unable to pay, and Empirical subsequently initiated the receivership proceeding, saying they were owed $33,419,371,06 as of January 1, 2025, with interest continuing to accrue.

The original proposal (left) and current proposal (right) for 7115 Yonge Street and 8-14 Grandview Avenue in Markam. (Arcadis)

“I verily believe the Debtor is insolvent and unable to fulfil its obligations to the Lender and the other creditors,” said Empirical in an affidavit. “It does not appear to have the financial capability to proceed with the since May of 2024 and the Debtor appears to be unable to make any payment on account of the Loan.”

Before the receivership application was granted, however, the two sides entered into a forbearance agreement delaying enforcement until June 2025. According to the forbearance agreement, the developer was in discussions with Metrolinx at the time about three temporary easements, and was also awaiting a 13-day OLT hearing in May 2025.

However, Terra Bona defaulted on the forbearance agreement, they were still unable to repay the loan, and the receivership application was recommenced and granted on December 1, 2025.

The Sale

In late-January 2026, the court-appointed Receiver then retained Lennard Commercial Realty to list the property, with Peter DeGuerre, Joshua Perlstein, and Paul Campbell serving as the listing team, beating out proposals by Cushman & Wakefield, CBRE, and Colliers.

“This offering represents a rare opportunity to acquire a high-density, transit-oriented development site with a Yonge Street address,” said Lennard Commercial Realty in its sales brochure. “With full approvals secured through the Ontario Land Tribunal (OLT) Order (Case No. OLT-24-000601) issued Nov 12, 2025, the site offers a rare opportunity to develop a landmark high-rise development in this highly accessible and sought-after North York corridor.”

According to a report prepared by the Receiver dated September 11, 2026, Lennard marketed the property, 28 interested parties reached the point of signing a confidentiality agreement, and a total of seven offers were received.

In June, the Receiver entered into a sale agreement with 2158046 Ontario Inc., which waived its conditions on August 19. The true purchaser was not identified, but a copy of the sales agreement included in court filings was signed by Shane Baghai, a luxury condo developer operated by the company’s namesake.

The purchase price was not disclosed, but the Receiver said Empirical was owed $39,167,304.23 as of August 24, 2026 and said “It is anticipated that Empirical will suffer a shortfall,” suggesting the purchase price was lower than the outstanding debt.

Comparable transactions Lennard cited in a report included the sales of 7-17 Nipigon Avenue for $26,623,000, the sale of 26-34 Nipigon Avenue for $19,350,000, and the sale of 41-47 Hendon Way for $15,350,000, all of which occurred in 2024 and 2025.

The sale to 2158046 Ontario Inc. was approved by the Ontario Superior Court on September 22.

items.title: Housing coalition outlines four demands ahead of B.C. election
items.description: Developers and affordable housing providers urge parties to restore planned investments and reduce development costs
items._ogDesc: Developers and affordable housing providers urge parties to restore planned investments and reduce development costs
items.body:
Market-rate developers and non-profit housing providers are joining forces to urge B.C.’s political parties to reduce the cost of building homes, warning that rising expenses and policy uncertainty are leaving projects stalled.

The Urban Development Institute (UDI), B.C. Non-Profit Housing Association (BCNPHA), Aboriginal Housing Management Association (AHMA) and Co-operative Housing Federation of B.C. (CHF BC) on Tuesday called on all parties to commit to four measures aimed at making housing development more financially viable.

The groups said the cost of building and financing homes in B.C. has exceeded what many buyers can afford and what governments are willing to subsidize for low- and moderate-income renters, resulting in projects failing to get off the drawing board.

“When market developers and non-profit housing providers are asking for the same thing, it should tell every party how serious the cost of delivery crisis is,” said Mike Drummond, CEO of UDI, in a statement.

The groups are asking the next provincial government to restore planned investments in non-profit, co-operative and Indigenous housing, allowing more than 5,000 affordable rental homes that were deferred following $1.4 billion in recent budget cuts to proceed.

“The projects are ready, but the land sits empty,” said Jill Atkey, CEO of the B.C. Non-Profit Housing Association.

“The people waiting for affordable housing cannot wait another budget cycle. The next government has an opportunity to restore the investment and get these homes built.”

The coalition also called on the government to co-invest remaining BC Rental Protection Funds with the Canada Rental Protection Fund to “continue protecting the affordability that already exists in the market.”

In addition, the groups urged the next government to finalize a federal-provincial agreement to reduce development cost charges and fund infrastructure needed to support new housing within 90 days of forming government.

The federal and provincial governments announced a 10-year partnership in June under which they would each contribute nearly $1.6 billion to reduce development charges for multi-unit housing by up to 50 per cent in priority communities and fund infrastructure.

“The details were not finalized before the election was called, so builders cannot price it into projects and municipalities cannot act on it,” said the coalition in a statement Tuesday.

Lastly, the groups called for a federal GST exemption on new homes for all eligible buyers rather than limiting relief to first-time purchasers. They pointed to Ontario’s expanded HST rebate program, announced in March, which temporarily eliminated the 13 per cent HST on eligible buyers of new homes valued at $1 million or less.

“The commitments made in 2024 need to translate into homes on the ground,” said Margaret Pfoh, CEO of the Aboriginal Housing Management Association, in a statement.

items._ogDesc: Canadians expect to buy their first home at 41, while nearly half of homeowners can’t afford their next move, an RBC poll finds.
items.body:
Canada’s housing ladder isn’t just hard to get on—nearly half of owners can’t afford to get off the first rung. RBC’s 2026 Home Ownership Poll looked at home buying expectations and financial constraints. The poll shows first-time buyers are getting older, and fewer owners can afford to upgrade. Meanwhile, the Bank of Mom and Dad is expanding its territory—literally, as multi-generational living returns.

Canada’s First-Time Buyers Expect To Buy Their First Home At 41

Canada’s first-time buyers will be on the back half of life’s golf course before they get into the market. Aspiring first-time owners plan to buy at 41 years old on average, 12 years later than current owners. That may be an optimistic number, as nearly half of them were unsure when they would be able to buy a home.

Becoming a homeowner is much harder than it was for past generations, said most (74%) of non-owners. Over 3 in 4 (77%) believe buying is harder than it was in the past, and 60% say traditional buyer advice is no longer true. Existing homeowners are likely to agree with that last point.

Canadian Homeowners Can’t Afford To Upgrade Their Starter Home

High home prices don’t just impact first-time buyers, it causes buyer gridlock. Modern housing markets are built around the concept of a property ladder. Homebuyers progressively move up the ladder, upgrading as they build equity. That process has been breaking down, as fewer people can afford to upgrade.

Nearly half (46%) of current owners want a larger or different home, but say it’s not financially realistic. Most (52%) say moving up from their first home is harder than expected, a problem the whole industry is about to feel. If existing starter home owners can’t buy the next rung, those sellers face reduced liquidity. At the same time, there are fewer starter homes for buyers to get onto the property ladder in the first place.

Aspiring first-time homebuyers are taking note and skipping the ladder. The survey found 74% are looking for a long-term home instead of a starter. Starting ownership 12 years later than average means very different property needs. Delaying their buy until the age of their peak earnings growth can help them afford to skip the starter. It also means starter homeowners will see their liquidity turn into their competition.

RBC senior mortgage specialist Brad Evjen suggests this may not always be the best strategy. “Buying a home you can stay in longer usually means stretching your budget further, so the math has to work in both directions,” he notes. He prefers to walk clients through monthly payments against what moving up in five years would cost.

Usually, the down payment problem is a bigger hurdle than the monthly payment. First-time buyers are increasingly tapping the Bank of Mom and Dad. However, not everyone’s parents are rich—some are actually looking for help with their own cost of living.

Multi-Generational Households Return With High Home Prices

Canada’s lack of affordability may soon reverse nuclear households to their pre-war roots. The survey found that 57% of prospective first-time buyers would consider multi-generational living—parents living with their adult children. However, it’s not just a first-time buyer thing—most buyers (53%), including those who currently own, would consider multi-generational living. Nearly half (44%) of all respondents, including those not in the housing market at all, would also consider the option.

Only a few years ago, it became normal for parents to help with a down payment. Now 29% of prospective first-time buyers say multi-generational buying is more a necessity than a choice. A problem that parents are receptive to—35% of homeowners say they’re prepared to sell and jointly buy with their kids to help them enter the market.

Canada’s housing ladder is difficult to enter—and getting onto it doesn’t guarantee you can climb it. Those looking to enter the market can’t do so until much later in life. At the same time, those who own are increasingly struggling to upgrade from their starter. Helping to bridge the gap are families pooling resources to buy what was considered normal for the last three generations.

items.title: B.C. home sales fall nine per cent in September amid interest rate speculation
items.description: VANCOUVER — Home sales in British Columbia dipped again in September, with the province's real estate board saying interest rate hike speculation weighed on the market.
items._ogDesc: VANCOUVER — Home sales in British Columbia dipped again in September, with the province's real estate board saying interest rate hike speculation weighed on the market.
items.body:
VANCOUVER — Home sales in British Columbia dipped again in September, with the province's real estate board saying interest rate hike speculation weighed on the market.

The British Columbia Real Estate Association says in a release that just over 5, 250 homes were sold last month, down about 9 per cent from the same month in 2025.

Home sales were about 26 per cent lower than the 10-year average for B.C. for the month of September.

The association says sales volume for residential transactions in B.C. last month was $4.9 billion, down 11 per cent from a year ago, while the average price on the Multiple Listing Service fell 2.4 per cent to just over $924,000.

Association chief economist Brendon Ogmundson says in a statement that the declines come after "an encouraging summer" where B.C. showed signs of recovery, but spiking oil prices have prompted speculation on whether the Bank of Canada will raise interest rates.

About 51,000 homes have been sold in B.C. so far in 2026, down about 6 per cent from the same period last year, with sales in September falling year-over-year in every region other than South Peace River and the Kootenays.

items.title: New Barrie Condo Blends Several Strategies To Create Affordability
items.description:
While some condo developers are pivoting to purpose-built rentals or opting to build larger, more expensive units amid a sluggish condo market, one Barrie developer is harnessing modular and standardized construction techniques, alongside housing incentive programs, to bring affordability back to the condo market.

“Own a condo for less than rent” promises Sean Homes’s 405 Essa project, slated for the west side of Essa Road, just north of the Ferndale and Veterans Drive intersection in south Barrie. It’s an impressive offer, with monthly payments, including mortgage, taxes, and condo fees starting at just $1,500 for a $249,990, 375-sq.-ft pre-construction studio.

Also on offer are a range of units including lofts, one-bedrooms starting at $399,990, one-bedrooms with either lofts or dens, two-bedrooms starting at $499,990, and two-bedrooms-plus-den units. While final pricing for some unit types is yet to be finalized, Sean Homes founder Sean Mason says he’s aiming to make 70% of the units affordable and priced under $425,000.

“This is housing for someone making $24 an hour,” he says. “That's somebody who is a construction labourer, a painter, a waitress, or a cook. Not, not a chef, but a cook. That's who I'm trying to serve.”

To help keep costs down, Mason adapted Barrie’s Development Charge (DC) waiver program — originally intended for rental developments offering at least 20% affordable housing in intensification corridors — to a for-sale condo project. To secure a full city fee waiver, Mason agreed to make 20% of the building affordable; however, because roughly 70% of the building's smaller units naturally qualify for Ontario’s automatic provincial DC exemption for affordable housing, the city waiver effectively covers the remaining 30% of market-rate units. Barrie also recently slashed its DCs by 50%, further reducing the cost of the project.

“So for an investment of around $1.5 million, they're getting approximately 90 affordable, for-sale condo units in the City of Barrie,” says Mason. “When I speak with staff, they say, ‘our return on investment here is amazing.’”

The other piece of the puzzle was leveraging modular and standardized construction. The development is being built using large cross-laminated mass timber panels that can be easily installed, saving time and money. “We order the largest panels they can fit on a truck,” says Mason. “So it's affordable. Because then when you're lifting pieces up, you're only lifting one big piece instead of three different smaller pieces.” He’s also importing standardized balconies from the UK that are so efficient, Mason says they can install one every 15 minutes.

New technologies help shave even more off the development’s bottom line. Interior source heat pumps cut down on energy costs, plasma phase change hot water technology means they don't have to install a central boiler or run lines throughout the entire building, and robotic parking stackers negate the need for additional levels underground that require more materials and time to construct.

The seven-storey mixed-use development will contain 134 residential units featuring sleek, modern interiors, and retail at ground level. Amenities include a lobby coffee bar, co-working lounge, a year-round sauna and snow lounge, and weekly boxing and yoga classes in the fitness studio.

Shovels will be in the ground this winter, pending a strong sales launch at the end of October, which Mason is confident will happen. Occupancy at 405 Essa is expected in two years.

OTTAWA — Statistics Canada says the total value of building permits issued in Canada in August rose $1.1 billion month-over-month to $13.6 billion, boosted by strength in the residential sector.

The agency says construction intentions for the homebuilding sector rose $1.1 billion to $8.5 billion in August.

The increase came as permits for multi-unit buildings rose to $5.8 billion, while the total value of permits for single-family homes edged down to $2.6 billion.

The value of non-residential building permits edged lower by $29.8 million to $5.1 billion in August.

The move came as plans for commercial construction fell $380 million to $2.2 billion, offset in part by a $317.3-million gain in the industrial sector which totalled $1.1 billion.

The institutional building component rose $32.9 million to $1.8 billion.

items.title: Vancouver opens the door to convertible balconies
items.description: Developers say retractable glass systems can make balconies more usable during the city’s rainy months
items._ogDesc: Developers say retractable glass systems can make balconies more usable during the city’s rainy months
items.body:
Having a balcony is nice for people who want to enjoy some fresh air without leaving home. But what about balconies that could be closed off to shield residents from Vancouver’s rain and wind, and reduce the noise from the streets below?

A number of companies and developers are introducing the concept to the region—convertible balconies that can be temporarily enclosed or opened, usually using retractable glass panels.

Vancouver city council recently updated its design guidelines to recognize fully retractable glass balcony systems. The changes will take effect Oct. 27, according to the city.

“Balconies with glass panels that slide, fold, or stack open can still be considered outdoor space, as long as the glass can be fully opened, the balcony is not permanently heated, and it continues to function primarily as a balcony rather than an indoor room,” the City of Vancouver said in a statement.

The City also approved removing restrictions on how much balcony space can be excluded from a building’s floor area calculations, effective Oct. 27, giving developers more flexibility to include larger balconies in new apartment buildings.

“These changes make it easier to build larger balconies and clarify that retractable glass weather screens can be used without the balcony being treated as enclosed indoor space, provided the guidelines are met,” the city said.

Some B.C. developers and companies are applauding the changes, saying convertible balconies give residents more flexibility in how they use their living space and could make balconies more usable.

“[It’s a] big deal … that Vancouver has recognized, like many other municipalities,” said Michael Geller, a Vancouver-based developer, real estate consultant and retired architect. He is working with Finnish firm Lumon Group to introduce retractable glass panels for balconies to B.C. and has been advocating for the concept for years.

Other municipalities, including Burnaby, North Vancouver, Langley, West Vancouver and Victoria, have already allowed the technology, according to Geller.

“Sometimes it's nice to have the window open and get the fresh air, and sometimes it's nice to close because it's a bit cold [or it's raining], and it's also quite noisy driving along,” he said.

“It really makes the balcony much more usable.”

Vancouver-based Concord Pacific Developments Inc. is building a three-building high-rise complex in the Metrotown area that’s scheduled for completion next year. One of the selling points for the project is its large convertible balconies, according to Terry Hui, president and CEO of Concord.

An 825-square-foot two-bedroom unit at Concord Metrotown, starting at about $1 million, has more than 500 square feet of outdoor space with retractable glass panels that Hui said would significantly increase residents’ living space.

“The market really likes it,” said Hui, noting that about 85 per cent of the roughly 1,400 units have been presold.

“Families are very excited about it as well, to be able to have the kids on the outside space while the parents try to maintain their sanity inside. …We have one buyer that's excited about having his office outside because he likes fresh air.”

Not appealing to cost-sensitive buyers

The convertible balcony offers residents more flexibility, but it remains a premium feature given the costs and housing affordability challenges in Metro Vancouver, according to industry insiders.

“I think it's a great idea and it's a great use of space,” said Mike Stewart, a Vancouver-based real estate agent and blogger. “It makes the balcony useful for more days of the year.”

He said he sees the product appealing to buyers who value large balconies and are willing to pay a premium for the units, but less attractive to average buyers because of the additional cost it adds to already-expensive homes in Metro Vancouver.

“It's a premium thing because the people who are price-sensitive are primarily not buying the bigger, higher-end, nicer units with the large balconies,” said Stewart.

“For smaller balconies, it doesn't really make sense to [install the system].”

Stewart said he could see the product becoming more popular in markets where activity is stronger and prices are rising, as buyers may be more willing to pay for upgrades. That, however, is not the case in Metro Vancouver right now.

Geller said cost is one of the main challenges to wider adoption of convertible balcony systems in the region. He did not disclose the specific price of installing Lumon’s retractable glass system but said it can range from several thousand dollars to more than $10,000.

“But the cost will come down as it becomes more common,” he said.

Given the current tax and regulatory framework for property development, it can be difficult for developers to make a profit selling small, inexpensive units because of the costs involved, so many choose to offer more features to target high-end buyers, according to Stewart.

The convertible balcony feature, as well as other features such as EV chargers, could help projects stand out in a softer market and give them a competitive advantage, he added.

“The market dynamic is for the developers to offer more to win market share in a smaller market,” said Stewart.

“If [buyers] have a choice between a big balcony that isn't convertible and a big balcony that is convertible, and maybe the price difference isn't much, they probably would choose the convertible balcony.”

Geller believes the City of Vancouver’s approval will help make convertible balconies a standard feature in new housing projects over time.

“I would suggest that just like air conditioning is becoming almost standard in many good quality high-rise buildings, 10 years from now, most new apartments will have it in Vancouver because it makes a lot of sense,” he said.

items.description:

The post Canada’s Housing Crash Rivals US In 2008, But The Pain Is Hidden: BMO appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canada’s home prices fell more than 20%, but BMO says population growth may have masked the economic pain of the housing crash.
items.body:
Canada’s housing crash is close to rivalling the early 2000s crash in the US. In contrast, Canada seems relatively unscathed, despite being a smaller economy that’s more dependent on housing. BMO’s chief economist notes the country is better positioned to avoid a financial crisis, but its pain avoidance is partly an illusion—hidden by Canada’s aggressive use of immigration.

Canadian Home Prices Are Following The US Housing Crash

Source: BMO Capital Markets; CREA.

The Canadian housing correction is following the same trajectory as the U.S., but with a different outcome. Home prices in Canada have dropped 20.5% from the early-2022 peak, compared with 26% during the U.S. bust. However, Canada avoided a comparable economic collapse—its real GDP grew at an annualized pace of 1.7% over the four years since prices started falling. That’s only slightly below the 2.0% average for this century, which is remarkable considering the country’s housing-dependent economy.

“This is arguably the most significant home price correction ever for Canada, and yet the economy has managed to avoid serious collateral damage from the deep decline,” explains BMO Chief Economist Douglas Porter.

He notes Canada has seen only one “traditional” recession in the past 35 years. That was the Global Financial Crisis, with 2020 being a very different policy-induced shutdown. He clarifies, “… it’s not as if recessions never happen, they are now just extremely rare events, and it takes a near cataclysm to cause a full-scale downturn.”

How? There’s some clear factors that helped mitigate the worst of the fallout—at least on the surface.

Stronger Borrowers And Rate Cuts Helped Contain The Fallout

The bank sees the brief period of peak home prices as one of the key differentiators. Porter notes prices surged 50% over the final two years, containing the damage to a relatively small pool. The correction is also largely contained in two provinces, leaving prices relatively unscathed for almost half the country. A substantial wealth cushion also helps limit spending cutbacks, while an aging population increasingly supports consumption through non-employment income such as pensions. In fact, seniors (aged 65+) represented over 1 in 5 (22.4%) dollars of consumption in 2025.

Source: BMO; Haver Analytics; Statistics Canada.

The bank also notes that the finances were stronger. Mortgage qualification hurdles, like the stress test, helped minimize the volume of overextended borrowers. Rate cuts began less than a year after rates peaked, softening the normalization shock. Overall, the headline data reveals an economy that’s darn near invincible.

Skeptical that a housing-based economy could survive a US-style housing correction with so little damage? There’s a good reason—the apparent escape may have been partly an illusion, according to Porter.

Canada Avoided A Financial Crisis, But It Didn’t Avoid The Pain

Porter believes Canada avoided the financial crisis, but avoiding the pain is partly an “illusion.” The population grew at an annualized pace of 2.8% over two years to early 2024, generally faster than GDP averaged. This helped to offset—possibly more than offset—any pullback in GDP. The economy grew, but the population grew faster—meaning less economic output per person, despite headline gains.

Source: BMO; Haver Analytics; Statistics Canada.

Measured per person, real GDP per capita fell in four of five quarters during the 2022-23 stretch, falling more than 2% peak-to-trough. Unemployment also climbed more than 2 percentage points over that period, a rare combination. Porter says this has only occurred a handful of times in the past 60 years—and only during official recessions.

Source: BMO; Haver Analytics; Statistics Canada.

“In other words, some of Canada’s Housing Houdini may have in fact been an illusion, not unlike the original act,” says Porter.

items.title: How Olivia Chow And Brad Bradford Plan To Address Toronto’s Housing Woes
items.description:
As the October 26 Toronto mayoral election approaches, the city’s housing and affordability crisis remains one of the most pressing issues among voters, and for good reason.

Fewer than 1 in 6 Torontonians can afford to buy a home in the city, minimum wage workers have to work 145 hours per month to afford the average asking rent for a one-bedroom apartment, and while the city pledged to facilitate 285,000 new homes by 2031 in 2022, it’s only achieved 32% of that goal as of this August.

Toronto’s top mayoral candidates — Incumbent Mayor Olivia Chow, and former urban planner and City Councillor Brad Bradford — both say they can put a good dent in Toronto’s housing and affordability woes, but they differ on how to pull it off. Here’s how Bradford and Chow plan to tackle the housing file:

Olivia Chow

City-led affordable housing

Under Chow’s lead, housing has shifted out from under the domain of the private market toward a more public, city-led development model. Since Chow took office in 2023, 5,271 city-owned housing units have broken ground, including 1,680 affordable units. Her plan is to continue building affordable and rental units via her public development model, with a goal of delivering 65,000 rent-controlled homes by 2030. She also wants to encourage development through new incentive programs that cut fees for developers in exchange for affordable units.

Cutting red tape

Chow champions zoning reforms that allow for more missing middle housing, including as-of-right multiplexes, and fast tracking transit-oriented developments. She’s also working to streamline the development review process with pre-approved building plans and expanding the online application process with automated checks and submissions. Chow has said efforts like these have made Toronto 80% faster at approving new housing. She has also eliminated development charges (DCs) for projects up to six units, created an incentive program that eliminates DCs for purpose-built rental housing, and played a central role in securing the $1.5 billion tri-governmental deal to lower DCs by 40%-60% in June.

Protecting tenants

Chow has promised a $2.15-million bad landlord task force under RentSafeTO, if re-elected. The task force would use enforcement officers and lawyers to investigate reports of neglectful landlords and buildings in disrepair. Fines paid by landlords and RentSafeTO funds would pay for the initiative.

Expanding taxes

Chow says she backs increasing taxes on vacant and luxury homes to fund affordable housing and prevent speculation. It’s a stance she has been consistent on. In 2023, she created the luxury property tax and voted to increase the vacant homes tax from 1% to 3%.

Brad Bradford

Private development

Bradford disagrees with Chow’s public builder model for delivering affordable housing, favouring partnering with experienced non-profit and market builders who he believes can build housing faster and cheaper than the City has.

Cutting red tape

As the former Chair of the Planning and Housing Committee, Bradford brought forward the Housing Action Plan to legalize gentle density, update urban design rules like eliminating the angular plane, and speed up approvals. If elected, he promises to continue updating city guidelines and streamlining the development review process, in part by increasing the use of technology. Bradford has also long called for the dropping of DCs to get shovels in the ground faster. He put forward a motion to lower DCs by 25% last March, which was rejected by Chow, and voted in favour of slashing DCs by 40% or 50% this June.

Renter strategy

Bradford is proposing a three-part plan to help renters: “Keep your home. Cool your home. Build more homes.” He wants to keep the existing renoviction by-law, but improve its enforcement by implementing a public dashboard to keep track of licenses and investigations and provide more funding for enforcement. He also wants to ensure renters have at least one cool room in their house, without any rent hikes to pay for it. Finally, Bradford promises clearer rules and earlier funding for non-profit rental builders instead of one-off negotiations for each site.

No to taxation

Bradford is against raising taxes on vacant and luxury homes, and has said he wants to keep costs down for all Torontonians. If elected, Bradford also promises to eliminate Toronto's Municipal Land Transfer Tax for homes valued at or below $1.1 million.

items.title: How An Ottawa Office Conversion Ended Up In Receivership
items.description:
An office-to-residential conversion project in Ottawa has been placed under receivership after the conversion commenced without the approval of the lender, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court.

The property is a seven-storey office building with 106,195 sq. ft of leasable space, located at 495 Richmond Road in Ottawa near Westboro Beach and the Ottawa River.

The building was previously owned by Artis REIT, which sold the building in September 2019 for $39,000,000 to an undisclosed buyer. (Artis REIT was absorbed by RFA Capital Inc. earlier this year.)

That buyer was Toronto-based DOV Capital, through Dov (495 Richmond) Limited, which financed the acquisition in part via a first-ranking mortgage from Addenda Capital Inc. — a subsidiary of insurance company Co-operators — in October 2019 for the principal amount of $30,947,000.

The loan was amortized over 25 years, and had an initial five-year term with a maturity date of December 7, 2024, with the interest rate set at 3.44%, and was guaranteed — with varying liability limits — by 1263191 Ontario Limited, Adarsan Holdings Limited, AMJ London Consulting Corporation, Dazco Family Holdings ULC, Dov Capital Corporation, The Friedman Family Foundation, Harvey Katz Holdings Ltd., Lindifam Realty Inc., Rolesco Management Limited, Shutam Canada Inc., and Sea Brim Investments Limited, according to court documents.

In November 2025, Regional Group submitted a site plan control application to convert the office building into a residential building with 143 units. Regional Group, however, does not appear to have an ownership interest in the property, and is identified in court filings as a manager of the property.

The Receivership

According to an affidavit sworn by an executive at Addenda Capital on September 2, the maturity date of the loan was extended several times: to March 7, 2025, September 7, 2025, and then March 7, 2026, before Addenda agreed to a final extension to September 7, 2026 to allow DOV Capital to refinance the loan.

During this extension period, DOV Capital was required to make interest-only payments amounting to the RBC Prime Rate + 2.00%, with a minimum rate of 6.45% per annum, but failed to make the payments in June, July, and August, defaulting on the extension agreement and loan.

On June 12, Addenda issued a formal demand for payment, claiming it was owed $25,798,415.18 with interest accruing at a daily rate of $4,593.20. The lender gave the borrower a deadline of June 22, 2026 to repay the loan, after which they would seek to enforce the loan, including the commencement of a receivership proceeding.

Around that same time, Addenda retained Brentwood Restructuring Services to inspect the property and assess the viability of a settlement DOV Capital had proposed. Brentwood found that the borrower had retained JBPA Developments Inc. and “The interior had been substantially altered and demolished, leaving principally only the concrete structure and building envelope intact,” according to Addenda.

Brentwood also found that JBPA had not been paid certain amounts, and that other trades had also not been properly paid.

Addenda says it “did not consent to the demolition and/or construction” and “is concerned that the conversion of the Real Property from an office building, that formed the basis of its security, to a vacant and partially demolished construction site materially affects the character, condition, marketability, and value of the Real Property.” They are also concerned about being left with a partially-demolished office building and that unpaid contractors may eventually register liens.

“Addenda has repeatedly requested financial and other information concerning the Real Property, including information regarding CMHC underwriting and the Debtor’s proposed redevelopment and financing plan for the Real Property,” they added. “The Debtor has failed to provide sufficient financial, operational, and project-specific information to date. As a result, Addenda has been unable to determine whether there is a viable alternative to enforcement that would preserve the Real Property, protect Addenda’s security, and provide for repayment of the Loan.”

Because of the above, Addenda believed the property could continue to deteriorate in value, hence the urgent need for a receivership. Addenda’s receivership application was granted on September 17, and the property is likely headed towards a court-ordered sales process.

Ottawa Office Conversions

According to an analysis published by commercial real estate services firm Avison Young last week, six Ottawa office buildings totalling nearly 750,000 sq. ft have been — or are in the process of being — converted into residential uses. Another 370,000 sq. ft is pending approval from the City of Ottawa.

“This wave of conversions is helping rebalance the office market by removing some of its least competitive inventory while creating more than 1,400 housing units in the downtown core,” said Avison Young. “The influx of new residents contributes to broader downtown revitalization efforts.”

(Avison Young)

The impact on the office market has also been “substantial,” as 9.0% of Class B and Class C office space inventory in downtown Ottawa has been removed since 2020 — a number that could further increase to 13.5%.

“Had these buildings remained in the leasing market, vacancy within the segment would likely be materially higher,” said Avison Young. “Under a scenario where a) the converted assets continued to operate at 50% occupancy; and b) absorption across Downtown Ottawa’s Class B and C inventory remained flat, vacancy rates would be roughly five percentage points higher by 2028 than current forecasts incorporating conversion activity.”

Avison Young notes that, although some office-to-residential projects have recently been put on hold or are shifting back to office uses, the conversion projects that are already underway will improve the competitiveness of existing office buildings and leave the office market as a whole on firmer footing.

With 495 Richmond Road already semi-demolished, it’s unclear whether the building can be reverted back to an office building, but a new developer that takes over the building could benefit from some of the conversion work already being completed, depending on their goals.

items.title: Bank of Canada Board launches process to fill external Deputy Governor position
items.description: The Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada has initiated a recruitment process to fill the external Deputy Governor position left vacant by the appointment of Nicolas Vincent as a full-time Deputy Governor.
items._ogDesc: The Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada has initiated a recruitment process to fill the external Deputy Governor position left vacant by the appointment of Nicolas Vincent as a full-time Deputy Governor.
items.body:
The Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada has initiated a recruitment process to fill the external Deputy Governor position left vacant by the appointment of Nicolas Vincent as a full-time Deputy Governor. The Board has formed a selection committee and retained recruitment firm Egon Zehnder to assist with the search process.

“The Bank has been operating in a rapidly changing and shock-prone economic environment, amid heightened uncertainty and longer-term structural change” said Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem. “It’s more important than ever to bring in policymakers with fresh perspectives and a diverse set of skills.”

The Bank created the role of external Deputy Governor in 2022 with the goal of bringing fresh and diverse perspectives to strengthen its monetary policy deliberations and financial stability assessments. External Deputy Governor appointments are part-time roles for a two-year term, with the possibility of extension for an additional one or two years. During their terms, external Deputy Governors contribute directly to the formulation of monetary policy, the assessment of financial stability risks, and the development of the Bank's strategic thinking on economic and financial matters. They also play an important role in the Bank's communications and outreach activities.

“As members of Governing Council, external Deputy Governors have demonstrated their value in bringing complementary experience and expertise to the table,” said Anne Whelan, Lead Independent Director. “The successful candidate will have the opportunity to further enrich Governing Council deliberations and contribute directly to economic and financial policy decisions affecting Canadians.”

The Bank’s selection committee is seeking outstanding candidates from a broad range of disciplines and backgrounds, with extensive senior-level experience in economics, finance, financial markets or related fields and the ability to assess and communicate complex economic and financial issues. Interested candidates are encouraged to review the Executive Brief for the role and contact Egon Zehnder to discuss their candidacy at: ExternalDG-SGexterne@egonzehnder.com

items.title: Bank of Canada unveils new vertical $20 bank note
items.description: Her Excellency the Right Honourable Louise Arbour, Governor General of Canada, and the Honourable Wayne Long, Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), joined Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem today at an event to unveil Canada’s new vertical $20 bank note featuring a portrait of His Majesty King Charles III.
items._ogDesc: Her Excellency the Right Honourable Louise Arbour, Governor General of Canada, and the Honourable Wayne Long, Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), joined Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem today at an event to unveil Canada’s new vertical $20 bank note featuring a portrait of His Majesty King Charles III.
items.body:
Her Excellency the Right Honourable Louise Arbour, Governor General of Canada, and the Honourable Wayne Long, Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), joined Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem today at an event to unveil Canada’s new vertical $20 bank note featuring a portrait of His Majesty King Charles III. This is Canada’s first bank note to feature His Majesty’s portrait and the first time in more than 70 years that a new monarch has appeared on the $20 denomination. The new note will gradually enter circulation in late February 2027.

“This new $20 bank note is striking, symbolic and secure,” said Governor Macklem. “The note’s advanced and dynamic security features are combined with images that reflect Canada’s beauty and its history. I hope it evokes pride in Canada and confidence in its bank notes.”

The portrait of his Majesty is surrounded by a floral and leafy tapestry inspired by the King’s lifetime dedication to the environment. The back of the note retains the Canadian National Vimy Memorial in France as a tribute to Canada’s contributions and sacrifices in military conflicts throughout its history.

Provincial and territorial floral emblems representing the 13 provinces and territories appear on the front of the note. A circular window, visible from both sides of the note, features plants that are culturally significant to Indigenous Peoples in Canada. The Bank’s Indigenous Advisory Circle collaborated on creating the design of this window.

This is the second bank note in the Vertical series. The first, the $10 note, features civil rights pioneer and businesswoman Viola Desmond.

The Bank also consulted with Canadians, government partners and a range of stakeholders including accessibility groups and organizations connected to the memorial at Vimy Ridge. Their input was instrumental in the development of the new $20 note.

Bank note security is integral to Canada’s currency and to the confidence of consumers and businesses that rely on cash. The new $20 note has security features never before used on Canadian currency that are easy to check and hard to counterfeit. The purple security stripe includes elements that spin, transform and pulse when the note is moved. Features like these will help the Bank maintain its technical advantage over counterfeiters and enable Canadians to easily authenticate $20 bank notes, the denomination they use most often. This ensures Canadians can use the new $20 note with confidence.

“The new $20 note reflects important parts of who we are as Canadians, honouring our Commonwealth roots and our ties with international allies,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “It honours our constitutional traditions through the portrait of His Majesty King Charles III and recognizes the service and sacrifice of Canadians through the Vimy Memorial, a symbol that continues to resonate across generations.”

“The new $20 bank note tells a distinctly Canadian story—one shaped by our natural beauty, our rich history and the enduring partnerships we have built around the world,” said Secretary of State Long. “It is a symbol Canadians can carry with pride.”

Before issuing the new note, the Bank will raise awareness among the public and other stakeholders. When introducing new notes, the Bank works closely with financial institutions, equipment manufacturers and the cash-handling industry to help ease the transition. This includes encouraging businesses that use bank note handling and processing equipment to contact their suppliers about any necessary machine adaptations. Retailers, law enforcement agencies and others will also be informed about the note’s design and security features, helping to maintain Canadians’ trust in their bank notes.

Remarks

Read the full remarks delivered during the unveiling of the new $20 bank note in Ottawa.

  • Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem
  • Governor General Louise Arbour

items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada today held its target for the overnight rate at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada today held its target for the overnight rate at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%.

The continuing conflict in the Middle East is keeping energy prices high. As well, new US tariffs and Canadian counter-measures have been announced following the breakdown of trade talks between Canada and the United States. Both situations remain fluid.

In the United States, economic growth continues to be solid, driven by consumer spending and AI-related investment. Growth in the euro area was stronger than expected in the second quarter, while China’s economy slowed. Overall, the global economy has shown resilience in the face of geopolitical headwinds, with growth broadly consistent with the July Monetary Policy Report (MPR) projection. With still-high oil prices and elevated margins for refined energy products, inflation in most countries remains high.

Financial conditions have tightened since July. Long-term bond yields have moved up globally, including in Canada. The Canadian dollar has appreciated slightly on US-dollar weakness.

As expected, Canadian economic activity strengthened in the second quarter, with GDP up by 3.3%, following very weak growth in the first quarter. While some of the recent strength reflected temporary factors, the pick-up in activity was broad-based. Consumption showed solid gains. Following several weak quarters, there was some rebound in housing activity. Exports and business investment were up sharply. Labour market conditions have improved in recent months, with the unemployment rate edging down to 6.4% in July. Still, demand for labour remains subdued and indicators point to continued excess supply in the economy.

Overall, recent data reaffirm Governing Council’s view of a broadening recovery in Canada’s economy. However, uncertainty is high and new US tariffs and threats of further action pose risks to the sustainability of the recovery.

CPI inflation has been hovering around 3% in recent months, mainly because of persistently higher gasoline prices. So far, there has been little evidence of higher energy prices spreading to other components of inflation: excluding gasoline, inflation was 2.2% and measures of core inflation remained close to 2% in July. However, with the Middle East conflict still ongoing and little progress reopening the Strait of Hormuz, upside risks to the Bank’s inflation forecast have increased. The longer that high oil prices and elevated refinery margins persist, the greater the risk of spillover to the prices of other goods and services. New US tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs will also raise costs for some businesses and could feed into consumer prices over time.

With the economy and inflation evolving broadly as forecast in the July MPR, Governing Council agreed to leave the policy rate unchanged. However, the upside risks to inflation have increased, while new tariffs make growth prospects more uncertain. Governing Council will assess the sustainability of the economic rebound and the outlook for inflation, and is prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed. The Bank remains committed to maintaining Canadians’ confidence in price stability through this period of global upheaval.

Information note

The next scheduled date for announcing the overnight rate target is October 28, 2026. The Bank’s next MPR will be released at the same time.

items.title: G7 2026 Cross-Border Coordination Exercise (CBCE)
items.description: The G7 Cyber Expert Group (CEG) successfully concluded its 2026 Cross-border coordination exercise (CBCE) on May 18, 2026. This exercise demonstrates the Group’s ongoing commitment to strengthening cyber resilience across the G7 financial sector.
items._ogDesc: The G7 Cyber Expert Group (CEG) successfully concluded its 2026 Cross-border coordination exercise (CBCE) on May 18, 2026. This exercise demonstrates the Group’s ongoing commitment to strengthening cyber resilience across the G7 financial sector.
items.body:
The G7 Cyber Expert Group (CEG) successfully concluded its 2026 Cross-border coordination exercise (CBCE) on May 18, 2026. This exercise demonstrates the Group’s ongoing commitment to strengthening cyber resilience across the G7 financial sector. A long-term exercise strategy has now been adopted to increase the frequency and consistency of these simulations, thereby enhancing preparedness across all jurisdictions.

Building on the success of the 2024 CBCE exercise, which aimed to strengthen the G7 financial authorities’ capacity to coordinate and communicate effectively in response to a major cross-border cyber incident affecting the financial sector, this year’s sessions tested key improvements identified through previous simulations and workshops focused on incident response, recovery, and crisis communication, further advancing collective preparedness. To enhance coordination among G7 financial authorities, the exercise simulated a large-scale cyber-attack across all G7 jurisdictions. The scenario brought together ministries of finance, central banks, bank supervisors, and market authorities, fostering a unified response.

Through these exercises, the G7 Cyber Expert Group seeks to reinforce the financial sector’s capacity to withstand cyber threats and reduce potential disruptions across G7 jurisdictions.

“As cyber threats continue to evolve, cooperation across G7 nations is more important than ever. Exercises such as this one strengthen our collective ability to respond to major cyber incidents, improve information sharing among financial authorities, and reinforce the resilience of the global financial system. I thank all participants for their continued commitment to this important work.”
- The Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue

This initiative enables financial authorities to further align and integrate the various operational and strategic components required for an effective response to cyber incidents.

In an increasingly interconnected world, cross-border coordination, incident response preparedness, and timely information sharing remain key G7 priorities. The G7 Cyber Expert Group continues to work and collaborate to address potential cyber threats to safeguard the stability and integrity of the global financial system.

“In our increasingly global financial system, countries can't address cyberthreats in isolation. Cross-border coordination exercises allow us to test and align our cyber security preparedness with domestic and international partners. This improves our resilience - both individually and collectively.”
- Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada

About the G7 Cyber Expert Group

The G7 Cyber Expert Group is responsible for coordinating cybersecurity policy and strategy across the G7 jurisdictions. Its mission is to enhance the cyber resilience of the financial sector by fostering preparedness, establishing a shared understanding of the threat landscape, and promoting unified approaches to risk mitigation.

Recent G7 Cyber Expert Group publications include:

  • G7 Cyber Expert Group Statement on AI and Cybersecurity (2025)
  • G7 CEG Reconnection Framework Best Practice (2025)
  • G7 Cyber Expert Group statement on transition to post-quantum cryptography (2026)

items.description: The Bank of Canada today published a report summarizing the feedback it received from stakeholders and the Canadian public during consultations on its monetary policy framework.
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada today published a report summarizing the feedback it received from stakeholders and the Canadian public during consultations on its monetary policy framework.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada today published a report summarizing the feedback it received from stakeholders and the Canadian public during consultations on its monetary policy framework.

Every five years, the Bank of Canada and the Government of Canada review and renew the agreement on Canada’s monetary policy framework. The agreement will be renewed before the end of 2026. In preparation, the Bank held consultations to gather views on inflation, monetary policy and on three key challenges to Canada’s economy that were the focus of the Bank’s research.

  • In a world with more adverse supply shocks affecting inflation dynamics and economic activity, how should monetary policy respond?
  • In a world more prone to volatility, how should the Bank assess and communicate about inflation? What measures of core inflation are most robust to structural changes in the economy?
  • How does monetary policy affect housing demand and supply, and how is inflation in shelter prices measured and interpreted for policy purposes?

Conversations were held in communities across the country to better understand Canadians’ recent experience with inflation and to hear their perspectives on monetary policy. The Bank also met with a broad group of stakeholders including members of the research community, the private sector and civil society.

The feedback the Bank received indicates that Canadians value the stability the framework provides. Support for maintaining flexible inflation targeting and the 2% inflation target was strong. At the same time, many participants expressed concerns about the high cost of living and housing affordability. They indicated that clear communication about the information the Bank uses to make interest rate decisions is key to fostering trust in the central bank.

“It was important for the Bank to hear from Canadians as part of this process because inflation and interest rate decisions affect their day-to-day lives,” said Governor Tiff Macklem. “I’m thankful to everyone who participated in these consultations and for the value these perspectives will bring to the renewal of our policy framework.”

Read the full report.

items.title: Bank of Canada joins BIS Project Agorá to test improvements in wholesale cross-border payments
items.description: The Bank of Canada announced today it is joining the Bank for International Settlements’ Project Agorá, an initiative exploring how tokenization could improve wholesale cross-border payments.
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada announced today it is joining the Bank for International Settlements’ Project Agorá, an initiative exploring how tokenization could improve wholesale cross-border payments.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada announced today it is joining the Bank for International Settlements’ Project Agorá, an initiative exploring how tokenization could improve wholesale cross-border payments.

The project has successfully tested the feasibility of a multi-currency unified ledger that enables atomic settlement of cross-border wholesale transactions. The Agorá prototype combines tokenized commercial bank deposits and wholesale central bank money on a programmable platform with the aim of improving the speed, efficiency, transparency and accessibility of international payments.

The project will continue to test the prototype and examine how an Agorá-type platform could operate within existing legal and regulatory frameworks, including rules on settlement finality as well as laws designed to counter money-laundering and terrorism financing.

Project Agorá brings together central banks and private sector financial institutions to experiment with next-generation payments infrastructure. It aligns with the Bank of Canada’s research focus on the evolution of payments and how emerging technologies can support a more efficient financial system.

“We know that the Canadian economy could benefit from innovation in cross-border payments,” said Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers. “Tokenization has the potential to make these payments faster, cheaper and more efficient and secure. Project Agorá is a unique opportunity to test the technology across several jurisdictions and currencies, with the participation of private sector financial institutions.”

The global project involves seven other central banks—the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Bank of England, Bank of France (representing the Eurosystem), Bank of Japan, Bank of Mexico, Swiss National Bank and Bank of Korea—and involves more than 40 financial institutions, including systemically important banks, payment service providers and clearing houses.

items.title: Bank of Canada Museum honours two Canadian educators for innovation in the classroom
items.description: Ethan McDonagh and Andrew Leong have won the Bank of Canada Museum’s 2026 Award for Excellence in Teaching Economics.
items._ogDesc: Ethan McDonagh and Andrew Leong have won the Bank of Canada Museum’s 2026 Award for Excellence in Teaching Economics.
items.body:
Ethan McDonagh and Andrew Leong have won the Bank of Canada Museum’s 2026 Award for Excellence in Teaching Economics. McDonagh is a Wilfrid Laurier University student completing a practicum at Northbrae Public School in London, Ontario. Leong teaches at Prince of Wales Secondary School in Vancouver, British Columbia.

They were chosen from nominations across Canada for lessons that helped students connect economics to contemporary issues. “What impressed the selection committee was how intentionally these lessons were designed for real-world understanding,” said Deputy Governor Sharon Kozicki. “Whether students were visualizing income distribution with beads or ‘travelling’ through global economies, the learning was active, inquiry-based and grounded in evidence. That’s what great economics education looks like.”

Ethan McDonagh (Grade 6, London, ON)

McDonagh designed an inquiry-based Grade 6 lesson that used coloured beads as data to explore income distribution, the value of labour and fairness. Working in pairs, students allocated 100 beads across 10 professions to show what they believed people should earn, then combined their results into a visual model. McDonagh then introduced gold beads representing actual Canadian income distribution for the same professions. Students compared their “should earn” models with the real data by graphing the two and calculating mean, median and mode. Using the poverty line as a reference point, students then had a rich discussion about basic needs and fairness. The class concluded with an $8 million redistribution challenge that asked students to defend their decisions.

Andrew Leong (Grade 12, Vancouver, BC)

Leong created a gamified project, called the Macroeconomic Venture Passport, that helps Grade 12 students learn macroeconomics by “travelling” through eight global economies and earning passport stamps. Each stop uses hands-on activities and simulations to explore real issues shaping today’s economies—such as artificial intelligence and automation in Japan, deforestation in the Amazon and Canada’s 2% inflation target. Students also tackled fiscal trade-offs through a budget-balancing game, seeing how policy choices can affect debt and everyday costs. By blending storytelling, data and mini-challenges, Leong helped students connect abstract macroeconomic concepts to daily life and understand Canada’s place in an interconnected global economy.

Each winner receives a trophy along with a personal cash prize of $1,000 and another $1,000 for their school.

Nominations for next year’s award will open in early 2027.
